title: Unconditional existence of one-way functions
open: Prove that a polynomial-time computable function family is hard to invert on a non-negligible fraction of randomly generated inputs, without assuming another computational hardness conjecture.
status: Foundational since the 1970s. Numerous candidates exist, but unconditional computational security remains unproved.
why: This would establish the foundations of computational cryptography rather than merely conditional constructions.
key_works: Boneh and Shoup, 2023, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*; MIT, 2025, *Open Questions* lecture.

title: One-way functions from P ≠ NP
open: Determine whether worst-case hardness expressed by P ≠ NP alone implies the existence of one-way functions.
status: Open for decades. Worst-case-to-average-case reductions face substantial barriers; worst-case hardness is not presently interchangeable with cryptographic average-case hardness.
why: This would connect the central complexity-theoretic conjecture directly to cryptographic security.
key_works: Akavia, Goldreich, Goldwasser, and Moshkovitz, 2005, *On Basing One-Way Functions on NP-Hardness*.

title: Key agreement from arbitrary one-way functions
open: Construct secure classical key agreement from arbitrary one-way functions, or establish an appropriately general impossibility beyond existing black-box separations.
status: Open since the 1980s. Oracle separations rule out broad black-box approaches, not every possible non-black-box construction.
why: This would bridge private-key and public-key cryptography.
key_works: Impagliazzo and Rudich, 1989, *Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations*; Barnum and Heath, 2026, *How to Steal Oblivious Transfer from Minicrypt*, ePrint 2026/113.

title: Collision-resistant hashing from arbitrary one-way functions
open: Determine whether general one-way functions suffice for collision-resistant hash families through constructions not excluded by black-box lower bounds.
status: Longstanding. Known separations distinguish collision resistance from the hashing properties routinely obtained from one-way functions.
why: Collision resistance supports commitments, authenticated data structures, and many proof systems.
key_works: Simon, 1998, *Finding Collisions on a One-Way Street: Can Secure Hash Functions Be Based on General Assumptions?*; Couteau, Farshim, and Mahmoody, 2021, *Black-Box Uselessness: Composing Separations in Cryptography*, ePrint 2021/016.

title: Injective one-way functions from general one-way functions
open: Construct injective one-way functions from arbitrary, potentially highly many-to-one, one-way functions without assuming additional hardness.
status: Open. Injective constructions follow from particular number-theoretic assumptions, but that does not give a general transformation.
why: Injectivity simplifies commitments, authentication, and cryptographic reductions.
key_works: Goldreich, Levin, and Nisan, 1995, *On Constructing 1-1 One-Way Functions*, ECCC TR95-029.

title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
open: Determine whether arbitrary one-way functions imply efficiently evaluable, length-preserving one-way permutations.
status: Longstanding. Definitions involving keyed families and restricted domains require care; those variants do not automatically settle permutations on all bit strings.
why: This would clarify whether permutation structure is an additional cryptographic assumption.
key_works: Goldreich, 2005, *On One-Way Permutations: A Clarification*; Goldreich, Levin, and Nisan, 1995, *On Constructing 1-1 One-Way Functions*.

title: Goldreich-generator security against unrestricted efficient distinguishers
open: Prove suitable polynomial-stretch Goldreich local generators pseudorandom against all polynomial-time distinguishers, under a clearly stated, independently motivated assumption.
status: Since Goldreich’s local-function proposal. Concrete attacks and restricted-model analyses constrain predicates and stretch, but do not establish unrestricted security.
why: Local pseudorandomness would enable exceptionally cheap cryptographic computation.
key_works: Couteau, Dupin, Méaux, Rossi, and Rotella, 2018, *On the Concrete Security of Goldreich’s Pseudorandom Generator*, ePrint 2018/1162.

title: Tight search-to-decision reductions for random local functions
open: Remove or substantially reduce sample, dimension, and advantage losses in reductions from distinguishing random local-function outputs to recovering their inputs.
status: Active. Tan–Vasudevan’s 2025–2026 reduction handles constant-arity predicates but still incurs quantitative overhead.
why: Better reductions would turn attack evidence into more reliable security estimates.
key_works: Tan and Vasudevan, 2025–2026, *Improved Search-to-Decision Reduction for Random Local Functions*, ECCC TR25-139.

title: Oblivious transfer from arbitrary public-key encryption
open: Determine whether the existence of arbitrary semantically secure public-key encryption implies oblivious transfer, without extra algebraic or structural assumptions.
status: Longstanding. Non-black-box developments do not provide a generic construction from every public-key encryption scheme.
why: Oblivious transfer supplies the foundation for general secure two-party computation.
key_works: Gertner, Kannan, Malkin, Reingold, and Viswanathan, 2000, *The Relationship Between Public Key Encryption and Oblivious Transfer*; Barnum–Heath, 2026, ePrint 2026/113.

title: Classical polynomial-time integer factorization
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Find a classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm for factoring arbitrary integers, or establish meaningful lower bounds in a sufficiently expressive computational model.
status: Open for decades. Quantum polynomial-time algorithms do not resolve the classical problem.
why: This would transform computational number theory and invalidate factoring-based cryptography.
key_works: Boneh and Shoup, 2023, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*; Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*.

title: RSA inversion versus factoring
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Prove or refute that efficiently inverting RSA on random messages implies efficient factorization of the RSA modulus, without restricting the adversary to a generic algebraic model.
status: Open since RSA’s introduction. Generic-ring equivalence results do not establish unrestricted equivalence.
why: This would determine whether RSA rests on factoring hardness or a potentially weaker assumption.
key_works: Aggarwal and Maurer, 2009, *Breaking RSA Generically Is Equivalent to Factoring*.

title: Computational Diffie–Hellman versus discrete logarithms
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Establish general conditions under which solving computational Diffie–Hellman permits efficient discrete-logarithm computation, ideally covering cryptographically relevant prime-order groups without auxiliary smoothness assumptions.
status: Open in general. Reductions exist under additional group-order and number-theoretic conditions.
why: This would clarify the exact assumption underlying Diffie–Hellman protocols.
key_works: Maurer, 1994, *Towards the Equivalence of Breaking the Diffie-Hellman Protocol and Computing Discrete Logarithms*, DOI 10.1007/3-540-48658-5_26.

title: Prime-field discrete logarithms below the number-field-sieve regime
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Find a general classical discrete-logarithm algorithm over large prime fields with asymptotic complexity substantially below the number-field-sieve regime.
status: Longstanding. Advances for small-characteristic fields do not automatically transfer to large prime fields.
why: Such an algorithm would change security estimates for finite-field cryptography.
key_works: Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*, discrete-logarithm and index-calculus chapters.

title: Non-generic attacks on ordinary prime-order elliptic curves
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Find an asymptotically sub-square-root classical discrete-logarithm algorithm for ordinary cryptographic elliptic curves without exploiting an already excluded special structure.
status: Open. Generic-group lower bounds do not exclude algorithms using the explicit curve representation.
why: This is a central unresolved security question for elliptic-curve cryptography.
key_works: Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*, elliptic-curve discrete logarithms.

title: Rigorous complexity analysis of practical number-field sieving
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Replace the principal smoothness and independence heuristics in practical number-field-sieve analyses with rigorous bounds that retain useful asymptotic and concrete estimates.
status: Longstanding. Practical algorithms and heuristic models are substantially more developed than unconditional analyses of their full pipelines.
why: This would make factoring-based security estimates less dependent on extrapolation.
key_works: Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*, factoring and index-calculus chapters.

title: Modular small roots beyond the Coppersmith bound
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: For general monic degree-\(d\) polynomials modulo an unknown-factorization composite \(N\), determine when roots larger than approximately \(N^{1/d}\) can be recovered efficiently.
status: Since the 1990s. Special polynomial structure permits improvements; a general extension remains unresolved.
why: This would sharpen the boundary of numerous partial-information attacks.
key_works: Coppersmith, 1997, *Small Solutions to Polynomial Equations, and Low Exponent RSA Vulnerabilities*, DOI 10.1007/s001459900030.

title: Rigorous multivariate Coppersmith criteria
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Give efficiently checkable conditions guaranteeing that lattice-generated multivariate polynomial relations yield all intended small roots, without heuristic algebraic-independence assumptions.
status: Since the 1990s. Successful cryptanalytic applications coexist with gaps between lattice reduction and guaranteed root extraction.
why: This would distinguish proved attacks from experimentally successful heuristics.
key_works: Coppersmith, 1997, *Small Solutions to Polynomial Equations, and Low Exponent RSA Vulnerabilities*; Boneh–Durfee, 1999, *Cryptanalysis of RSA with Private Key \(d\) Less than \(N^{0.292}\)*.

title: Optimal RSA reconstruction thresholds from random leaked bits
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Determine sharp polynomial-time reconstruction thresholds when randomly positioned bits of specified RSA secret components are revealed, separating information-theoretic identifiability from algorithmic recovery.
status: Active since the 2000s. The 2009 reconstruction work exploits redundancy across RSA key components; thresholds depend strongly on which components leak.
why: This would quantify the damage caused by partial memory disclosure.
key_works: Heninger and Shacham, 2009, *Reconstructing RSA Private Keys from Random Key Bits*, ePrint 2008/510.

title: The \(d<N^{1/2}\) small-private-exponent RSA target
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Determine whether balanced RSA with sufficiently small private exponent \(d<N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) can always be broken efficiently under appropriate standard parameter conditions.
status: Boneh–Durfee’s historical \(N^{0.292}\) milestone leaves a substantial gap to the \(N^{1/2}\) target.
why: This would settle a prominent boundary in RSA cryptanalysis.
key_works: Boneh and Durfee, 1999–2000, *Cryptanalysis of RSA with Private Key \(d\) Less than \(N^{0.292}\)*, DOI 10.1109/18.850673.

title: Parameter-tight classical worst-case reductions for LWE
open: Obtain classical worst-case-to-average-case reductions for cryptographically useful Learning With Errors parameters without the dimension, modulus, or approximation losses that weaken concrete interpretations.
status: Quantum and classical reductions exist, but under different parameter tradeoffs.
why: This would strengthen the connection between deployed parameters and worst-case lattice hardness.
key_works: Regev, 2005/2009, *On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography*; Brakerski et al., 2013, *Classical Hardness of Learning with Errors*, arXiv:1306.0281.

title: Fine-grained hardness at cryptographic lattice approximation factors
open: Prove quantitatively strong hardness for lattice approximation regimes actually used by cryptographic reductions, with explicit exponential-time consequences.
status: Major progress exists, but public-key and secret-key applications reach different approximation regimes and encounter reduction barriers.
why: This would support security claims more informative than asymptotic polynomial-time hardness.
key_works: Aggarwal et al., 2022, *Lattice Problems Beyond Polynomial Time*, arXiv:2211.11693.

title: Tight reductions for binary and sparse-secret LWE
open: Relate small-secret LWE to standard LWE with losses tight enough to explain observed concrete security across sparsity, modulus, and sample count.
status: Reductions and specialized attacks exist; empirical behavior can differ materially from generic LWE estimates.
why: Small secrets are valuable optimizations whose security cost must be understood.
key_works: Chen, Chua, Lauter, and Song, 2020, *On the Concrete Security of LWE with Small Secret*, ePrint 2020/539.

title: Complete accounting for the MLWE–LWE hardness gap
open: Characterize and tightly bound all practically relevant attack advantages obtained from module and ring symmetries, rather than treating structured instances as equivalent unstructured LWE.
status: A 2026 analysis identifies concrete gaps, including much larger effects for sparse-secret settings than for standardized ML-KEM parameters.
why: This directly affects structured-lattice parameter selection.
key_works: Hou, Jiang, and Ogilvie, 2026, *Careful with the Ring! Concrete Hardness Gaps Between LWE and MLWE*, DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-35377-1_15; ePrint 2026/279.

title: General-lattice foundations for ring-lattice assumptions
open: Establish useful reductions connecting the hardness of structured ideal/module lattices to general lattices, or precisely characterize unavoidable structural separations.
status: Structured worst-case foundations exist, but they are not equivalent to worst-case hardness over all lattices.
why: This would clarify what additional trust is introduced by algebraic compression.
key_works: Regev, 2005/2009, *On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography*; Hou–Jiang–Ogilvie, 2026, *Careful with the Ring!*.

title: Predictive BKZ cost models with calibrated uncertainty
open: Build models predicting attack success and total BKZ cost across unseen dimensions and lattice distributions, with validated uncertainty intervals rather than a single heuristic estimate.
status: Experimental studies have found instances easier than older estimators predicted; extrapolation remains central.
why: Security levels depend on these extrapolations.
key_works: Chen et al., 2020, *On the Concrete Security of LWE with Small Secret*, ePrint 2020/539.

title: Sharp unique-SVP attack thresholds for cryptographic embeddings
open: Explain when embedded LWE lattices yield their unusually short target vector, including the effects of secret distribution, embedding factor, and block size.
status: Empirical success thresholds need not match estimates derived from generic random-lattice heuristics.
why: Better thresholds could either expose weak parameters or remove unnecessary conservatism.
key_works: Chen et al., 2020, *On the Concrete Security of LWE with Small Secret*, ePrint 2020/539.

title: Optimal time–space tradeoffs for lattice sieving
open: Determine optimal classical SVP-sieving tradeoffs among exponential running time, memory, preprocessing, and success probability under explicit models.
status: Many sieve variants improve particular tradeoffs; a complete optimality theory is absent.
why: Memory constraints can change which attack is economically or physically feasible.
key_works: Ducas, 2017/2018, *Shortest Vector from Lattice Sieving: A Few Dimensions for Free*, ePrint 2017/999; Micciancio, *Lattice Sieving* research bibliography.

title: Realistic quantum lattice-sieving costs
open: Translate quantum sieve improvements into complete fault-tolerant resource estimates, including quantum memory access, routing, error correction, and classical preprocessing.
status: Quantum algorithmic improvements continue through 2026; query or gate asymptotics alone do not settle implementable advantage.
why: Post-quantum security depends on credible attacker resource models.
key_works: Engelberts et al., 2025–2026, *An Improved Quantum Algorithm for 3-Tuple Lattice Sieving*, arXiv:2510.08473.

title: Circular security of useful LWE encryption schemes
open: Prove the circular-security properties needed by practical bootstrapping constructions from plain LWE, without assuming those properties separately.
status: A persistent gap despite extensive key-dependent-message security results for particular schemes and function classes.
why: This would strengthen foundations for fully homomorphic encryption and related advanced primitives.
key_works: Micciancio and Vaikuntanathan, 2024, *SoK: Learning with Errors, Circular Security, and Fully Homomorphic Encryption*, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-57728-4_10.

title: Succinct LWE at application-useful widths
open: Establish hardness of succinct LWE in the intermediate-width regimes needed by applications, between known insecure narrow regimes and wider regimes reducible to ordinary LWE.
status: Explicitly active in 2026; the parameter gap is central to newer succinct cryptographic constructions.
why: This could validate or refute a foundation for compact commitments and encryption.
key_works: Wu, 2026, *Lattice Assumptions with Hints: Succinct LWE and Decomposed LWE*, July 2026 lecture.

title: SIS hardness for correlated succinct-LWE matrices
open: Determine whether the correlated matrices used in succinct-LWE constructions support the required short-integer-solution hardness, and with what quantitative losses.
status: Identified as a separate assumption-level question in the 2026 treatment.
why: LWE hardness alone does not automatically justify every commitment or proof application.
key_works: Wu, 2026, *Lattice Assumptions with Hints: Succinct LWE and Decomposed LWE*.

title: Worst-case foundations for decomposed and succinct LWE
open: Derive the relevant hinted or decomposed distributions from established worst-case lattice problems, rather than introducing their hardness independently.
status: Open in the application-relevant regimes discussed in 2026.
why: This would separate a powerful construction framework from its currently stronger assumptions.
key_works: Wu, 2026, *Lattice Assumptions with Hints: Succinct LWE and Decomposed LWE*.

title: Optimal classical information-set-decoding exponents
open: Determine optimal asymptotic and concrete tradeoffs for information-set decoding across code rate, target weight, memory, and preprocessing.
status: Improvements remain active in 2026; no general optimality characterization is known.
why: These algorithms underpin security estimates for code-based cryptography.
key_works: Yu et al., 2026, *Progressive Sieving-Style Information-Set Decoding Algorithm*, ePrint 2026/633.

title: End-to-end quantum decoding resource estimates
open: Identify the best physically realizable quantum decoding attacks after accounting for reversible circuits, memory, error correction, and classical list construction.
status: Quantum information-set-decoding algorithms exist, but asymptotic speedups are not complete hardware cost estimates.
why: This is necessary for defensible post-quantum code parameters.
key_works: Kachigar and Tillich, 2017, *Quantum Information Set Decoding Algorithms*, arXiv:1703.00263.

title: Goppa-code indistinguishability at cryptographic parameters
open: Characterize the computational distinguishability of public binary Goppa-code representations from comparable random codes, including whether distinguishers can yield useful key recovery.
status: Structural attacks constrain some code families; this does not amount to a general break of Classic McEliece.
why: It would clarify the security consequences of hidden algebraic structure.
key_works: Alagic et al., 2025, *Status Report on the Fourth Round of the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization Process*, NISTIR 8545, DOI 10.6028/NIST.IR.8545.

title: Exact security cost of quasi-cyclic code structure
open: Quantify all relevant gains from cyclic symmetries, multiple equivalent targets, and amortized preprocessing in attacks on quasi-cyclic code-based schemes.
status: Structural efficiency is established; comprehensive concrete accounting remains an active cryptanalytic task.
why: Compact keys should not be priced as though they came from fully random codes.
key_works: Alagic et al., 2025, NISTIR 8545; Yu et al., 2026, *Progressive Sieving-Style Information-Set Decoding Algorithm*.

title: Certified rare-event decoding-failure bounds
open: Produce tight, independently reproducible upper bounds on decoding failures in code-based KEMs, including adversarially influenced inputs and implementation deviations.
status: Failure probabilities are security-critical but often far below direct Monte Carlo reach.
why: Rare failures can affect both reliability and chosen-ciphertext security.
key_works: Alagic et al., 2025, NISTIR 8545, sections on code-based candidates and HQC.

title: Concrete MinRank security of UOV-family schemes
open: Establish reliable attack costs for UOV and compressed variants against modern MinRank, algebraic, and hybrid attacks across proposed parameter sets.
status: Active in 2026, with new key-recovery analyses changing the relevant attack landscape.
why: Multivariate signatures depend on more than generic quadratic-system hardness.
key_works: Furue et al., 2026, *Key Recovery Attacks on UOV Using \(p^\ell\)-Truncated …* (full title verify), DOI 10.1007/978-3-032-35398-6_10.

title: Safe public-key compression for multivariate signatures
open: Reduce UOV-family public keys substantially while retaining independently analyzed resistance to attacks exploiting the compression structure.
status: Proposed engineering target: a tenfold reduction against a fixed uncompressed baseline without reducing the target security level.
why: Large public keys impede otherwise attractive signature schemes.
key_works: Kipnis, Patarin, and Goubin, 1999, *Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar Signature Schemes*; NIST, ongoing *Additional Digital Signature Schemes* evaluation.

title: Fröberg’s conjecture for generic forms
open: Prove the predicted Hilbert series for ideals generated by generic homogeneous forms in the unresolved general parameter regimes.
status: Open since 1985. Numerous degrees, variable counts, and special cases are settled; the general conjecture is not.
why: It informs the algebraic regularity assumptions underlying polynomial-system complexity estimates.
key_works: Nenashev, 2017, *A Note on Fröberg’s Conjecture for Forms of Equal Degrees*, DOI 10.1016/j.crma.2017.01.011; Trung, arXiv:1803.04997.

title: Proving semi-regularity assumptions for random Boolean systems
open: Prove sharp high-probability algebraic regularity statements for random quadratic systems over \(\mathbb F_2\), sufficient to justify cryptanalytic solving-time estimates.
status: Algorithms with strong conditional bounds and supporting experiments exist; these are not unconditional typical-case analyses.
why: It would make multivariate security estimates mathematically firmer.
key_works: Bardet, Faugère, Salvy, and Spaenlehauer, 2013, *On the Complexity of Solving Quadratic Boolean Systems*, arXiv:1112.6263; DOI 10.1016/j.jco.2012.07.001.

title: Tight hardness of supersingular isogeny-path problems
open: Determine the best classical and quantum complexity of the precise path-finding and endomorphism problems used by surviving isogeny constructions.
status: SIDH/SIKE’s failure does not settle every isogeny assumption; problem distributions and auxiliary information must be distinguished.
why: It would establish which isogeny structures remain credible foundations.
key_works: Alagic et al., 2025, NISTIR 8545; Aardal et al., 2025, *Optimized One-Dimensional SQIsign Verification on Intel and Cortex-M4*.

title: Fully audited constant-time SQIsign signing
open: Deliver a complete signing implementation whose secret-dependent arithmetic, sampling, memory behavior, and exceptional paths satisfy a verified leakage model.
status: Constant-time four-dimensional lattice-reduction work addresses an important subroutine, not automatically the entire implementation.
why: Compact signatures are insufficient if signing leaks the private key.
key_works: Hanyecz et al., 2025, *Constant Time Lattice Reduction in Dimension 4 with Application to SQIsign*.

title: Embedded SQIsign verification with a tenfold resource reduction
open: Reduce total verification energy or latency tenfold relative to a pinned optimized embedded implementation, preserving parameters and counting memory and preprocessing.
status: Proposed moonshot; optimized Intel and Cortex-M4 verification provides a concrete 2025 baseline.
why: It would make compact post-quantum signatures more attractive on constrained devices.
key_works: Aardal et al., 2025, *Optimized One-Dimensional SQIsign Verification on Intel and Cortex-M4*, DOI 10.46586/tches.v2025.i1.497-522.

title: An eight-bit APN permutation
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Construct an almost-perfect-nonlinear permutation of \(\mathbb F_2^8\), or prove none exists.
status: The six-bit example does not extend the existence result to eight bits; major families and structural approaches have been excluded.
why: It would provide an optimal-differential permutation at the ubiquitous byte size.
key_works: Calderini, Sala, and Villa, 2017, *A Note on APN Permutations in Even Dimension*, DOI 10.1016/j.ffa.2017.02.001.

title: APN permutations in infinitely many even dimensions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Construct an infinite family of APN permutations in even dimensions greater than six, or establish an obstruction ruling such families out.
status: Open. Generalized Kim-type constructions have substantial negative results rather than a general solution.
why: This would settle whether the six-bit phenomenon is exceptional.
key_works: Chase and Lisonek, 2020, *Kim-Type APN Functions Are Affine Equivalent to Gold Functions*, arXiv:2009.05937.

title: The exceptional APN conjecture
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Classify polynomials that remain APN over infinitely many extension fields, resolving the conjectured restriction to Gold and Kasami–Welch types up to the relevant equivalence.
status: The general problem remains; special degree families have been eliminated or classified. Recent special-case resolutions must not be mistaken for the full conjecture.
why: It would classify indefinitely extensible optimal differential constructions.
key_works: Aubry et al., 2022–2023, *Polynomials with Maximal Differential Uniformity and the Exceptional APN Conjecture*, arXiv:2207.13945.

title: Complete CCZ classification of quadratic eight-bit APN functions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Enumerate all quadratic APN functions on eight bits up to CCZ equivalence, with machine-checkable completeness and inequivalence certificates.
status: Large collections of new examples exist, but a catalogue of examples is not a completeness proof.
why: A complete census would test structural conjectures and improve construction methods.
key_works: Beierle and Leander, 2021/2022, *New Instances of Quadratic APN Functions*, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 68, 670–678; Bergen Boolean-function tables.

title: Infinite quadratic APN families with non-classical Walsh spectra
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Construct an infinite family of quadratic APN functions whose Walsh spectra are non-classical, rather than isolated finite-dimensional examples.
status: Explicitly identified as a major remaining question in the 2026 revision of the cited work.
why: It would reveal structural diversity beyond the dominant known families.
key_works: Bénéteau, Goluboff, Kölsch, and Vaghasiya, 2025–2026, *On the Walsh Spectra of Quadratic APN Functions*, arXiv:2510.12008.

title: Sharp bounds on bent components of quadratic APN functions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Determine the maximum number of bent component functions of a quadratic APN map in each even dimension, with matching constructions or stronger impossibility bounds.
status: New nontrivial bounds appeared in the 2025–2026 work; sharpness remains unresolved in important regimes.
why: This links optimal differential behavior to linear-cryptanalysis resistance.
key_works: Bénéteau et al., 2025–2026, *On the Walsh Spectra of Quadratic APN Functions*, Open Problem 6.2, arXiv:2510.12008.

title: An eight-bit APN function with only 21 non-bent components
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Construct an eight-bit quadratic APN function attaining the proposed extremal amplitude distribution, equivalently the specified 21 nontrivial non-bent components, or prove impossibility.
status: Explicit unresolved instance highlighted in Open Problem 6.1 of the cited 2026 revision.
why: It would decide whether a new geometric lower bound is attained.
key_works: Bénéteau et al., *On the Walsh Spectra of Quadratic APN Functions*, arXiv:2510.12008, §6.

title: Maximum Boolean nonlinearity in odd dimensions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Determine the maximum nonlinearity of Boolean functions for unresolved odd numbers of variables, and its asymptotic behavior.
status: Longstanding; constructions and upper bounds do not coincide in general.
why: This determines optimal resistance to affine approximation.
key_works: Carlet, 2021, *Boolean Functions for Cryptography and Coding Theory*, DOI 10.1017/9781108606806, chapter “Open Questions.”

title: Asymptotic enumeration of bent functions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Obtain matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds for the number of bent Boolean functions, ideally identifying the leading growth term.
status: Large explicit families and counting bounds exist, but general enumeration remains unresolved.
why: It would measure how much of the optimal-nonlinearity landscape known constructions cover.
key_works: Carlet, 2021, *Boolean Functions for Cryptography and Coding Theory*, DOI 10.1017/9781108606806.

title: Exact differential–linear tradeoff frontiers for permutations
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Determine attainable pairs of differential uniformity and vectorial nonlinearity for permutations in unresolved dimensions, including proof of unattainability between known constructions.
status: Partial bounds and families exist; a full attainable-region description does not.
why: It would replace trial-and-error S-box selection with proven design frontiers.
key_works: Carlet, 2021, *Boolean Functions for Cryptography and Coding Theory*.

title: Sharp resilience–degree–nonlinearity tradeoffs
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Determine the best attainable nonlinearity at prescribed variable count, correlation-immunity order, balance, and algebraic degree.
status: Classical inequalities constrain the region, but many parameter combinations lack matching constructions.
why: These tradeoffs govern robust combining and filtering functions.
key_works: Carlet, 2021, *Boolean Functions for Cryptography and Coding Theory*, chapter “Open Questions.”

title: A substantial single-key attack on full AES-128
open: Find a full-round, single-key AES-128 key-recovery attack with a substantial advantage over exhaustive search under explicitly bounded data and memory.
status: Biclique cryptanalysis gives a historical slight theoretical improvement, not a practical break.
why: It would reveal structure not captured by current security assessments.
key_works: Bogdanov, Khovratovich, and Rechberger, 2011, *Biclique Cryptanalysis of the Full AES*, ePrint 2011/449.

title: Full AES-256 attacks outside the related-key model
open: Obtain a substantial full-round AES-256 attack in the ordinary single-key model, rather than relying on adversarial access to related keys.
status: Related-key results and small biclique advantages do not settle this target.
why: The ordinary deployment model is the relevant boundary for many applications.
key_works: Bogdanov, Khovratovich, and Rechberger, 2011, *Biclique Cryptanalysis of the Full AES*, ePrint 2011/449.

title: Full ChaCha20 cryptanalysis below generic key search
open: Find a valid full-round ChaCha20 key-recovery or distinguishing attack beating the corresponding generic bound under realistic data limits.
status: Research attacks continue to target much smaller round counts; those results are not full-ChaCha20 breaks.
why: ChaCha’s deployment makes its remaining security margin consequential.
key_works: Wang et al., 2026, *Enhanced Differential-Linear Cryptanalysis of ChaCha Based on Bit Puncturing*, ePrint 2026/1837.

title: Extending strong ChaCha attacks to eight rounds
open: Extend the best differential-linear and bit-puncturing approaches to an eight-round ChaCha256 key-recovery attack with nontrivial total advantage over exhaustive search.
status: The cited 2026 work reports attacks on seven and 7.5 rounds, with respective estimated times \(2^{142.08}\) and \(2^{242.02}\).
why: This probes the boundary of current ARX cryptanalytic techniques.
key_works: Wang et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/1837.

title: Full SHA-256 collisions below birthday complexity
open: Construct collisions for full, untruncated SHA-256 with total work substantially below the generic \(2^{128}\) scale.
status: Reduced-round and modified-initial-state results do not solve the standard-function problem.
why: Collision resistance underpins signatures, commitments, and content addressing.
key_works: NIST, 2015, *Secure Hash Standard*, FIPS 180-4.

title: Full SHA-256 preimages below generic search
open: Find preimages of independently specified SHA-256 outputs with a substantial classical advantage over generic \(2^{256}\)-scale search.
status: A distinct problem from collision finding; reduced-round preimage results do not settle it.
why: It tests a separate security property used by commitments and hash-based constructions.
key_works: NIST, 2015, *Secure Hash Standard*, FIPS 180-4.

title: Full SHA3-256 collisions below birthday complexity
open: Find collisions in the standardized full-round SHA3-256 function with substantially less work than generic birthday search.
status: Security analyses of reduced-round permutations or nonstandard sponge settings are not full-function collisions.
why: This would test whether the concrete permutation introduces exploitable structure beyond ideal-sponge analysis.
key_works: NIST, 2015, *SHA-3 Standard: Permutation-Based Hash and Extendable-Output Functions*, FIPS 202.

title: Full SHA3-256 preimages below generic search
open: Recover a preimage of a specified full SHA3-256 digest with a substantial classical advantage over generic search.
status: Separate from collisions, distinguishers, and reduced-round permutation attacks.
why: Preimage security is a foundational assumption for many higher-level constructions.
key_works: NIST, 2015, FIPS 202.

title: Full standardized Ascon-AEAD128 security margin
open: Find meaningful full-round attacks on standardized Ascon-AEAD128, or materially strengthen concrete bounds for specified attack classes and usage limits.
status: The 2025 standard fixes a particular variant; attacks on earlier or reduced variants require careful translation.
why: Lightweight security needs margins compatible with constrained implementations.
key_works: NIST, 2025, *Ascon-Based Lightweight Cryptography Standards for Constrained Devices*, SP 800-232.

title: Learned cryptanalysis that transfers to full-strength targets
open: Demonstrate a reproducible learned attack on a full-strength standardized primitive that beats the best matched non-learning attack after counting training, data, and inference.
status: Gohr’s 2019 work established important reduced-round results, not general full-round superiority.
why: It would determine whether machine learning adds cryptanalytic power rather than benchmark-specific speedups.
key_works: Gohr, 2019, *Improving Attacks on Round-Reduced Speck32/64 Using Deep Learning*, ePrint 2019/037.

title: Interpretable and transferable neural distinguishers
open: Extract mathematical features explaining successful neural distinguishers, then predict which round extensions, keys, and cipher variants preserve their advantage.
status: Learned distinguishers can exploit information beyond a selected differential, but understanding and transfer remain separate objectives.
why: Explanation could turn empirical successes into reusable cryptanalytic techniques.
key_works: Gohr, 2019, *Improving Attacks on Round-Reduced Speck32/64 Using Deep Learning*; accompanying implementation.

title: Independently checkable certificates for automated attack searches
open: Produce portable certificates that an automated differential, linear, or algebraic search found an optimal result within its declared model.
status: Proposed infrastructure target: separate solver trust, model correctness, and cryptanalytic validity.
why: A solver’s output is not by itself a proof of a cipher’s security margin.
key_works: Bellini et al., 2023, *Boosting Differential-Linear Cryptanalysis of ChaCha7 with MILP*; Gohr, 2019, ePrint 2019/037.

title: Unbounded FHE from plain LWE
open: Construct fully homomorphic encryption supporting unbounded iterative computation from plain LWE without an additional circular-security assumption or a depth bound fixed at key generation.
status: Leveled FHE from LWE is established; that is not the same statement.
why: It would close a central assumption gap in general encrypted computation.
key_works: Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan, 2011/2014, *Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption from (Standard) LWE*; Micciancio–Vaikuntanathan, 2024, *SoK: Learning with Errors, Circular Security, and Fully Homomorphic Encryption*.

title: Two orders of magnitude cheaper programmable bootstrapping
open: Reduce both per-operation latency and energy by 100× against a pinned optimized CPU baseline at the same concrete security and failure probability.
status: Proposed moonshot. TFHE and hardware accelerators provide substantial progress, but throughput must not be confused with single-operation latency.
why: Bootstrapping remains a major cost in nonlinear encrypted computation.
key_works: Chillotti et al., 2020, *TFHE: Fast Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus*, ePrint 2018/421; Van Beirendonck et al., 2022, *FPT*, arXiv:2211.13696.

title: Measured full-system FHE accelerator efficiency
open: Establish reproducible energy and latency measurements on fabricated hardware that include host work, transfers, memory, key loading, and complete application execution.
status: Proposed benchmark gap. Architectural projections and kernel measurements cannot substitute for these full-system results.
why: It would reveal whether accelerator gains survive deployment overhead.
key_works: Geelen et al., 2022, *BASALISC*, arXiv:2205.14017; Jiang, Lou, and Joshi, 2022, *MATCHA*, arXiv:2202.08814.

title: Compact bootstrapping keys without displaced costs
open: Reduce bootstrapping-key storage tenfold relative to a pinned current implementation without losing security or increasing total evaluation cost enough to erase the benefit.
status: Proposed joint optimization target; compression, decomposition, and recomputation trade storage against other resources.
why: Key material can dominate memory and deployment feasibility.
key_works: Chillotti et al., *TFHE*, ePrint 2018/421; Bossuat et al., 2024–2025, *Security Guidelines for Implementing Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2024/463.

title: Efficient circuit privacy for approximate homomorphic encryption
open: Hide evaluated circuits and intermediate numerical behavior while preserving useful accuracy and avoiding prohibitive noise growth in approximate encryption.
status: Approximate, circuit-private, and multiparty notions require careful distinctions; newer constructions do not eliminate every efficiency tradeoff.
why: Data privacy alone does not protect proprietary models or private computations.
key_works: Kluczniak and Santato, 2025, *On Circuit Private, Multikey and Threshold Approximate Homomorphic Encryption*; CKKS research discussion, 2026.

title: Optimal protection against adaptive approximate-output leakage
open: Characterize the minimum perturbation or protocol restrictions needed when an adversary adaptively observes approximate decrypted outputs.
status: Li–Micciancio demonstrated that exposed approximation errors can undermine naïve security interpretations; this is not a ciphertext-only break of CKKS.
why: Real applications return numerical answers, not merely ciphertexts.
key_works: Li and Micciancio, 2021, *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533; DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-77870-5_23.

title: Robust malicious multiparty approximate decryption
open: Make threshold approximate decryption secure against malformed shares, adaptive requests, dropout, and numerical leakage while retaining useful accuracy and throughput.
status: Relevant primitives exist; the proposed target combines their security and operational requirements.
why: Distributed key ownership should not introduce a decryption oracle or silent numerical corruption.
key_works: Kluczniak–Santato, 2025, *On Circuit Private, Multikey and Threshold Approximate Homomorphic Encryption*; Li–Micciancio, 2021.

title: End-to-end verified numerical error in FHE compilers
open: Certify application-level error from source semantics through approximation, quantization, rescaling, bootstrapping, and final decryption, including adversarially chosen valid inputs.
status: Proposed verification target; cryptographic parameter guidance alone does not prove numerical correctness.
why: An encrypted wrong answer remains wrong.
key_works: Bossuat et al., 2024–2025, *Security Guidelines for Implementing Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2024/463.

title: Verifiable FHE with near-native evaluation cost
open: Prove correct encrypted execution against a malicious evaluator with less than 10% additional end-to-end cost on a declared workload suite.
status: Proposed moonshot; generic proof-system composition establishes feasibility, not this overhead target.
why: Confidentiality does not ensure an outsourced computation was performed correctly.
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, *Scalable, Transparent, and Post-Quantum Secure Computational Integrity*, ePrint 2018/046; Chillotti et al., *TFHE*.

title: Efficient persistent encrypted RAM computation
open: Support long-running, dynamically updated encrypted memory with hidden access patterns, crash recovery, and substantially sublinear per-access overhead in realistic workloads.
status: FHE, PIR, and ORAM supply components; their persistent, verified integration remains a distinct systems target.
why: Real programs use mutable memory rather than fixed arithmetic circuits alone.
key_works: Larsen–Nielsen, 2018, *Yes, There Is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!*, ePrint 2018/423; Li et al., 2023–2024, *Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval*.

title: General encrypted inference within tenfold plaintext cost
open: Achieve at most 10× end-to-end cost for a declared, representative inference suite while preserving model utility, input privacy, and a fixed security level.
status: Proposed moonshot, not a claim that every specialized model lacks efficient private evaluation.
why: It would make confidential inference broadly deployable rather than task-specific.
key_works: Chillotti et al., *TFHE*, ePrint 2018/421; Jiang, Lou, and Joshi, 2022, *MATCHA*, arXiv:2202.08814.

title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted secret sharing
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Prove superpolynomial worst-case share-size lower bounds for general, potentially nonlinear, perfect secret-sharing schemes.
status: The worst-case **linear** exponent gap was resolved in 2026; unrestricted nonlinear lower bounds remain a different problem.
why: It would establish fundamental limits on implementing arbitrary access policies.
key_works: Nir, 2026, *Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*, ECCC TR26-146.

title: Explicit access structures requiring very large nonlinear shares
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Exhibit explicit, efficiently describable access structures with strong lower bounds against all perfect secret-sharing schemes.
status: Counting-style worst-case results and linear lower bounds do not supply this explicit unrestricted result.
why: Explicit hardness reveals which real policy structures are intrinsically expensive.
key_works: Nir, 2026, *Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*, ECCC TR26-146.

title: Near-zero active-security overhead for large MPC workloads
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Bring actively secure computation within 10% of a matched semi-honest implementation across a declared workload suite, counting preprocessing and failed executions.
status: Proposed moonshot; extensive protocol engineering has reduced costs but does not establish a universal small-overhead result.
why: Deployments should not have to trade away malicious-adversary protection.
key_works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, DOI 10.1145/3372297.3417872.

title: Optimal arithmetic–Boolean conversion in malicious MPC
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Determine tight communication and preprocessing costs for conversions, comparisons, truncation, and bit decomposition across different rings and adversary thresholds.
status: edaBits deliver major improvements, but do not establish optimality over all parameter regimes.
why: These conversions often dominate mixed numerical and logical workloads.
key_works: Escudero, Ghosh, Keller, Rachuri, and Scholl, 2020, *Improved Primitives for MPC over Mixed Arithmetic-Binary Circuits*, ePrint 2020/338.

title: Crash-safe, non-reusable MPC preprocessing
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Build a distributed preprocessing lifecycle that provably never reuses correlations after crashes, rollback, concurrent consumers, or partial commit.
status: Proposed infrastructure target beyond the algebraic correctness of triples or correlated bits.
why: Reusing one-time correlations can destroy security.
key_works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; Escudero et al., 2020, *Improved Primitives for MPC over Mixed Arithmetic-Binary Circuits*.

title: MPC under long-lived membership churn and mobile compromise
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Maintain a formally specified corruption threshold through participant replacement, refresh, downtime, and recovery without silently accumulating compromised shares across epochs.
status: Proactive and adaptive techniques exist; a complete operational implementation is the proposed target.
why: Real multiparty services outlive individual machines and administrators.
key_works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography* project and call.

title: Fast sparse-LPN correlation functions without a random oracle
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Retain the concrete efficiency of new sparse-LPN pseudorandom correlation functions while removing their random-oracle dependence.
status: The September 2026 construction provides a strong concrete baseline in the random-oracle model.
why: It would improve the foundations of locally generated MPC correlations.
key_works: Braun, Couteau, Melissaris, Riahinia, and Sadeghi, 2026, *Fast Pseudorandom Correlation Functions from Sparse LPN*.

title: Plain-LWE correlation functions matching broad DCR functionality
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Obtain comparably efficient, locally evaluatable correlation functions over broad arithmetic domains from plain unstructured LWE, with explicit security and setup guarantees.
status: DCR-based constructions and Ring-LWR approaches provide important partial alternatives; “PCFs from standard assumptions” is no longer the open question.
why: It would combine flexible correlations with post-quantum foundations.
key_works: Dutta, Kohl, Roy, and Scholl, 2026, ePrint 2026/2030; Hasler, Reisert, and Küsters, 2025, *Pseudorandom Correlation Functions from Ring-LWR*, ePrint 2025/1637.

title: Recoverable malicious setup for correlation services
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Extend correlation-function setup to a durable multiparty service with explicit honest-majority assumptions, malicious-input checks, restart safety, and unambiguous epoch changes.
status: Two-round distributed setup exists for important 2026 PCFs; full service recovery is a separate proposed target.
why: Setup failures must not create correlated-key reuse or undetected bias.
key_works: Dutta et al., 2026, *New Pseudorandom Correlation Functions and Exponent VRFs from DCR*, ePrint 2026/2030.

title: Fairness classification beyond symmetric Boolean outputs
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Characterize which general finite-output or asymmetric-output two-party functionalities admit complete fairness, with efficient protocols for every positive case.
status: Symmetric Boolean-output functions, including randomized ones, have a complete characterization; that solved case must be excluded.
why: It would identify when abort-based insecurity is fundamental rather than an implementation choice.
key_works: Asharov, Beimel, Makriyannis, and Omri, 2024, *Complete Characterization of Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation of Boolean Functions*, DOI 10.1137/18M1232656.

title: General NP SNARGs from plain LWE
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Construct succinct noninteractive arguments for general NP from plain LWE with clearly specified soundness, setup, and succinctness, without an additional strong commitment assumption.
status: SNARGs for P and stronger-assumption constructions do not settle this target.
why: It would provide a major new foundation for general succinct verification.
key_works: Choudhuri, Jain, and Jin, 2021–2022, *SNARGs for P from LWE*; Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, ePrint 2025/2328.

title: Function-statistically-binding commitments from weaker assumptions
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Construct function vector commitments with the binding properties needed for the new standard-model Micali-SNARG framework from substantially weaker assumptions.
status: The September 2026 framework identifies this commitment primitive as a concrete remaining cryptographic target.
why: It could remove a principal bottleneck in standard-model succinct arguments.
key_works: Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, *Micali’s SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*, ePrint 2025/2328.

title: Adaptive soundness for the new Micali-SNARG framework
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Extend the cited construction’s nonadaptive soundness to adaptive statement selection while preserving its assumption profile and succinctness.
status: The current framework explicitly establishes nonadaptive soundness.
why: Real applications commonly choose statements after seeing public parameters.
key_works: Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, *Micali’s SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*, ePrint 2025/2328.

title: Post-quantum recursion matching pairing-based practicality
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Match a pinned pairing-based recursive proof system’s proof size, verification latency, and prover cost using post-quantum assumptions and comparable security.
status: Post-quantum transparent proofs exist; simultaneous practical parity is a stronger proposed target.
why: Recursion is central to scalable proof-carrying computation.
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046; Kothapalli, Setty, and Tzialla, 2021–2022, *Nova*, ePrint 2021/370.

title: Tenfold smaller transparent proofs without hidden regressions
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Reduce transparent proof bytes tenfold against a fixed baseline while holding security, prover memory, verification cost, and trusted-setup requirements constant.
status: Proposed multiobjective moonshot rather than a claim that proof-size improvements have stopped.
why: Network and storage costs often determine whether proofs are usable.
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, *Scalable, Transparent, and Post-Quantum Secure Computational Integrity*, ePrint 2018/046.

title: Low-memory proving for very large computations
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Prove a declared hundred-million-step workload within a one-gigabyte working-memory budget and less than twice the time of an unrestricted-memory baseline.
status: Proposed target; streaming, recursion, and recomputation techniques address different parts of the tradeoff.
why: It would broaden proving beyond high-memory servers.
key_works: Kothapalli and Setty, 2023, *HyperNova: Recursive Arguments for Customizable Constraint Systems*, ePrint 2023/573.

title: Restart-safe recursive proof pipelines
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Preserve transcript binding, witness integrity, and unique step ordering across retries, parallel workers, checkpoints, and restored prover state.
status: Proposed systems target beyond the algebraic soundness of an individual folding scheme.
why: A correct proof primitive can still be embedded in an unsound computation pipeline.
key_works: Kothapalli–Setty–Tzialla, *Nova*, ePrint 2021/370; Kothapalli–Setty, *HyperNova*, ePrint 2023/573.

title: Characterizing standard-model Fiat–Shamir applicability
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Give useful necessary and sufficient conditions identifying which interactive argument families admit secure explicit Fiat–Shamir instantiations.
status: General instantiation is impossible; recent positive frameworks isolate additional structural properties rather than eliminating the barrier universally.
why: It would guide protocol design before an insecure transformation is deployed.
key_works: Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, *Micali’s SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*, ePrint 2025/2328.

title: Tight concrete post-quantum security for deployed Fiat–Shamir systems
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Obtain reductions tight enough to justify practical parameter choices under quantum oracle access, including multi-proof, adaptive, and recursive use.
status: Quantum-random-oracle proof techniques establish important possibilities, but concrete losses and composition must be analyzed per system.
why: “Post-quantum” is not a complete concrete security estimate.
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046; Guan–Yogev, 2025–2026, ePrint 2025/2328.

title: Verified compilation from program semantics to proof relations
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Prove that a production compiler’s generated constraints exactly encode source-language semantics, including overflow, memory, exceptional behavior, and nondeterministic inputs.
status: Proposed end-to-end target; soundness of PLONK or another backend does not establish correctness of the relation supplied to it.
why: An underconstrained circuit can prove the wrong statement perfectly.
key_works: Gabizon, Williamson, and Ciobotaru, 2019, *PLONK*, ePrint 2019/953; Kothapalli–Setty, 2023, *HyperNova*.

title: Cross-implementation malformed-proof corpus
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Build a maintained, versioned corpus covering noncanonical encodings, invalid subgroup elements, transcript ambiguity, boundary arithmetic, and recursive-proof edge cases.
status: Proposed data target with differential testing across independent implementations.
why: It would expose discrepancies invisible to valid-proof benchmarks.
key_works: Gabizon et al., 2019, *PLONK*, ePrint 2019/953; Kothapalli et al., *Nova*, ePrint 2021/370.

title: Indistinguishability obfuscation from plain LWE
subfield: Obfuscation, functional encryption, and advanced access control
open: Construct indistinguishability obfuscation for general polynomial-size circuits from plain LWE without circular security or additional independent assumptions.
status: iO from combinations of well-founded assumptions is established; circular-secure LWE suffices in another line. Plain LWE remains the sharper target.
why: It would consolidate an exceptionally powerful primitive onto one major assumption.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai, 2020–2021, ePrint 2020/1003; Brakerski et al., 2020–2022, *Factoring and Pairings Are Not Necessary for iO*, ePrint 2020/1024.

title: Practical general-purpose indistinguishability obfuscation
subfield: Obfuscation, functional encryption, and advanced access control
open: Obfuscate nontrivial general circuits with independently analyzed security and executable artifacts small and fast enough for ordinary machines.
status: Proposed moonshot; existence constructions do not constitute practical general-purpose software protection.
why: It would enable applications currently confined to theoretical feasibility.
key_works: Jain, Lin, and Sahai, 2020–2021, *Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*, ePrint 2020/1003.

title: Collusion-resistant general functional encryption from plain LWE
subfield: Obfuscation, functional encryption, and advanced access control
open: Construct public-key functional encryption for general circuits, secure against unbounded polynomially many colluding function keys, from plain LWE with useful compactness.
status: General functional encryption follows from stronger combinations of assumptions; that does not settle this single-assumption target.
why: It would support fine-grained computation on encrypted data.
key_works: Jain, Lin, and Sahai, 2020–2021, *Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*, ePrint 2020/1003.

title: Practical functional encryption beyond narrow algebraic functions
subfield: Obfuscation, functional encryption, and advanced access control
open: Implement general-circuit functional encryption with independently reviewed security and tractable key generation, ciphertext size, and decryption for substantial circuits.
status: Proposed engineering target; efficient special-purpose inner-product systems do not solve general-circuit practicality.
why: It would let data owners release computed answers without releasing the underlying data.
key_works: Garg et al., 2013, *Candidate Indistinguishability Obfuscation and Functional Encryption for All Circuits*, ePrint 2013/451.

title: Witness encryption from plain LWE
subfield: Obfuscation, functional encryption, and advanced access control
open: Construct witness encryption for general NP statements from plain LWE, without routing through stronger obfuscation assumptions.
status: General witness-encryption feasibility under stronger assumptions does not establish this target.
why: It would support encryption controlled by publicly specified computational witnesses.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai, 2020–2021, ePrint 2020/1003; Wu, 2026, *Lattice Assumptions with Hints*.

title: Succinct circuit access control without stronger hinted assumptions
subfield: Obfuscation, functional encryption, and advanced access control
open: Obtain the compact circuit-level access-control and registration capabilities enabled by newer hinted-lattice assumptions from plain LWE with comparable asymptotic efficiency.
status: The 2026 landscape distinguishes these stronger assumptions from established LWE.
why: It would strengthen the foundations of scalable encrypted authorization.
key_works: Wu, 2026, *Lattice Assumptions with Hints: Succinct LWE and Decomposed LWE*.

title: Dynamic stateless-client PIR with near-polylogarithmic work
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Support independently initialized clients querying a dynamically updated database with very small client state and near-polylogarithmic online server work, counting update and preprocessing costs explicitly.
status: Preprocessing and hintless PIR advance different tradeoffs; single-client ORAM does not automatically solve this multi-client setting.
why: It would make private retrieval economical for large shared services.
key_works: Li, Micciancio, Raykova, and Schultz-Wu, 2023–2024, *Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval*, ePrint 2023/1733.

title: Tenfold lower communication for practical hintless PIR
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Reduce total query-plus-response communication tenfold against a pinned hintless-PIR baseline while preserving security, answer size, and server-work constraints.
status: Proposed moonshot; hintless PIR itself already exists.
why: Communication can dominate mobile and wide-area private queries.
key_works: Li et al., 2023–2024, *Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval*, ePrint 2023/1733; accompanying implementation.

title: Cheap malicious-response verification for post-quantum PIR
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Verify answer correctness and database-version binding with less than 10% overhead over a matched post-quantum PIR baseline.
status: Proposed target; query privacy alone does not prevent omission, stale answers, or fabricated records.
why: Private retrieval should not require trusting server honesty.
key_works: Li et al., *Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval*; Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046.

title: Privacy-preserving maintenance of shared PIR preprocessing
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Refresh reusable preprocessing after updates without exposing client interests or allowing a malicious server to give selectively inconsistent database versions.
status: Proposed lifecycle target; preprocessing efficiency and update consistency must be measured together.
why: Static-query benchmarks do not establish a secure continuously updated service.
key_works: Li et al., 2023–2024, *Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval*; Melara et al., 2015, *CONIKS*.

title: Private multi-client writes with durable consistency
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Combine private reads and writes with malicious-server security, concurrent clients, crash recovery, and an explicit linearizability or fork-consistency guarantee.
status: Proposed integration problem; privacy and consistency mechanisms individually do not establish their joint contract.
why: Private databases must remain correct under ordinary distributed failures.
key_works: Larsen–Nielsen, 2018, ePrint 2018/423; Melara et al., 2015, *CONIKS*.

title: Tight lower bounds for offline ORAM
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Determine the optimal overhead of offline oblivious RAM in general computational models, distinguishing it from the online setting.
status: Strong online logarithmic lower bounds are established; they do not automatically resolve offline access sequences.
why: It would map where batching and advance knowledge can fundamentally help.
key_works: Larsen and Nielsen, 2018, *Yes, There Is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!*, ePrint 2018/423.

title: Concurrent ORAM without security-destroying recovery shortcuts
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Build a concurrent ORAM implementation whose position-map, stash, eviction, and recovery behavior remain oblivious under adversarial scheduling and crashes.
status: Proposed systems target beyond single-execution bandwidth analysis.
why: Recovery paths can expose accesses even when normal operations are oblivious.
key_works: Larsen–Nielsen, 2018, *Yes, There Is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!*, ePrint 2018/423.

title: Quantitative utility–leakage frontiers for searchable encryption
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Characterize the minimum leakage necessary to achieve specified search costs, and translate leakage into adversarial reconstruction success under explicit auxiliary-information models.
status: Leakage-abuse attacks show that seemingly modest leakage can be highly revealing; universal quantitative frontiers remain absent.
why: This would make encrypted-search security comparable across designs.
key_works: Cash, Grubbs, Perry, and Ristenpart, 2015, *Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption*, DOI 10.1145/2810103.2813700.

title: Dynamic volume hiding with low amortized padding
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Hide update, response-volume, and search-pattern leakage in dynamic encrypted databases with substantially less padding and bandwidth than worst-case fixed-size access.
status: Padding frameworks and forward/backward privacy address parts of the problem, not every joint tradeoff.
why: Volume patterns can reveal data despite ciphertext security.
key_works: Bost and Fouque, 2017, *Thwarting Leakage Abuse Attacks against Searchable Encryption—A Formal Approach and Applications to Database Padding*, ePrint 2017/1060.

title: Composable leakage budgets for long query histories
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Develop leakage accounting that remains meaningful under adaptive queries, evolving auxiliary knowledge, and combinations of several encrypted-data services.
status: Per-operation leakage descriptions are established tools; they do not automatically give an interpretable lifetime disclosure budget.
why: Small repeated disclosures can accumulate into near-complete reconstruction.
key_works: Cash et al., 2015, *Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption*; Bost–Fouque, 2017, ePrint 2017/1060.

title: Efficient output-oblivious encrypted joins
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Execute dynamic joins while hiding access patterns and sensitive intermediate cardinalities, with costs characterized against explicit output-size leakage allowances.
status: Proposed database target; merely encrypting records does not hide relational execution structure.
why: Joins are essential to useful databases and unusually leakage-prone.
key_works: Bost–Fouque, 2017, ePrint 2017/1060; Cash et al., 2015, *Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption*.

title: Verified SQL semantics for private query engines
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Verify that private execution preserves SQL semantics, including NULLs, duplicates, collation, overflow, ordering, and transaction visibility.
status: Proposed correctness target; cryptographic security does not establish semantic equivalence to the reference database.
why: Silent semantic changes can invalidate decisions made from protected data.
key_works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; Boldyreva and Tang, 2021, *Privacy-Preserving Approximate k-Nearest-Neighbors Search that Hides Access, Query and Volume Patterns*.

title: Billion-vector private nearest-neighbor search
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Support a billion-vector mutable collection with hidden access, query, and volume patterns, malicious-result checks, and a declared subsecond latency target.
status: Proposed scaling target; pattern-hiding approximate nearest-neighbor search already exists.
why: It would enable private retrieval over modern embedding databases.
key_works: Boldyreva and Tang, 2021, *Privacy-Preserving Approximate k-Nearest-Neighbors Search that Hides Access, Query and Volume Patterns*, ePrint 2021/816.

title: Transferable encrypted-database leakage benchmarks
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Build public benchmark suites with realistic, time-evolving auxiliary data and held-out workloads that measure actual reconstruction risk rather than attack success on one convenient dataset.
status: Proposed data target motivated by demonstrated leakage-abuse attacks.
why: It would prevent misleading claims based on weak or mismatched attackers.
key_works: Cash et al., 2015, *Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption*, ePrint 2016/718.

title: Compact post-quantum aggregation at practical verification cost
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Aggregate thousands of independently signed messages into a small proof with post-quantum security, no hidden trusted setup, and verification costs competitive with classical aggregation.
status: Proposed joint target; generic proof aggregation and particular aggregate constructions do not automatically achieve all requirements.
why: It would reduce certificate, ledger, and distributed-system authentication costs.
key_works: NIST, ongoing *Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization*; Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046.

title: Practical dynamic threshold post-quantum signatures
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Support dealerless generation, signing, refresh, and participant replacement with malicious security and low communication for standardized post-quantum signatures.
status: Active standardization and research; an interoperable lifecycle is stronger than a stand-alone threshold-signing protocol.
why: Long-lived keys should not require a single machine or static committee.
key_works: NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography* project and NISTIR 8214C call.

title: Crash-safe threshold-signature nonce management
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Prove that no nonce or presigning material can be reused across concurrency, retries, rollback, backup restoration, or coordinator equivocation.
status: Proposed implementation-security target; protocol proofs assume an appropriate randomness and state lifecycle.
why: One lifecycle mistake can expose a threshold signing key.
key_works: Komlo and Goldberg, 2020, *FROST: Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures*, ePrint 2020/852.

title: Proactive threshold refresh with auditable epoch boundaries
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Preserve a precise mobile-adversary security guarantee while participants refresh shares asynchronously and old, offline, or restored participants rejoin.
status: Proactive techniques exist; the proposed target is an auditable implementation of their epoch and erasure assumptions.
why: Refresh is ineffective if compromised shares silently accumulate across epochs.
key_works: Komlo–Goldberg, 2020, *FROST*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography*.

title: Practical post-quantum blind issuance
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Provide blind-signature or credential issuance with small messages, malicious-issuer security, unlinkability, and post-quantum assumptions at mobile-scale latency.
status: Proposed practicality target; pairing-based selective-disclosure systems provide a useful classical baseline.
why: Anonymous payments, credentials, and rate-limited services need efficient issuance.
key_works: Sonnino et al., 2018–2019, *Coconut: Threshold Issuance Selective Disclosure Credentials with Applications to Distributed Ledgers*, arXiv:1802.07344.

title: Robust batch verification for post-quantum signatures
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Obtain batch-verification speedups with tight soundness and efficient isolation of invalid signatures under adversarially chosen batches.
status: Proposed optimization target; benign all-valid throughput is not the relevant worst-case guarantee.
why: A small number of invalid submissions should not erase all batching gains.
key_works: NIST, *Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization* and additional signature evaluation.

title: Practical post-quantum verifiable delay functions
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Construct a VDF with credible post-quantum sequentiality, compact proofs, fast verification, and an explicit assumption weaker than simply assuming the whole desired primitive.
status: Classical unknown-order-group constructions are major milestones but do not establish post-quantum security.
why: It would support durable delay-based protocols after quantum migration.
key_works: Boneh, Bonneau, Bünz, and Fisch, 2018, *Verifiable Delay Functions*, ePrint 2018/601; Boneh et al., 2018, *A Survey of Two Verifiable Delay Functions*, ePrint 2018/712.

title: Hardware-robust sequentiality estimates for VDFs
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Bound realistic attacker speedups from custom arithmetic, pipelining, energy expenditure, and parallel preprocessing for concrete VDF parameters.
status: Mathematical sequentiality assumptions do not directly specify wall-clock advantage across hardware generations.
why: Protocol deadlines depend on actual delay, not abstract operation counts alone.
key_works: Boneh et al., 2018, *Verifiable Delay Functions*, ePrint 2018/601; Wesolowski, 2018–2019, *Efficient Verifiable Delay Functions*, ePrint 2018/623.

title: Transparent unknown-order parameter generation with stronger guarantees
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Give tighter foundations for public generation of hard unknown-order groups, explicitly accounting for biased parameter selection and hidden structural advantages.
status: Class-group VDFs avoid an RSA-modulus trapdoor ceremony, but their concrete hardness still depends on the chosen distribution.
why: “Transparent” setup should not conceal an unexamined parameter-generation assumption.
key_works: Wesolowski, 2018–2019, *Efficient Verifiable Delay Functions*, ePrint 2018/623.

title: Tight time-lock guarantees under heterogeneous hardware
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Characterize achievable real-time release intervals when honest and adversarial evaluators have different hardware, including impossibility bounds and measurable calibration assumptions.
status: Proposed theory-and-measurement target; an exact universal wall-clock delay cannot be inferred from a sequential-step count.
why: It would prevent time-lock applications from promising stronger timing guarantees than their assumptions support.
key_works: Boneh et al., 2018, *Verifiable Delay Functions*; Freitag et al., 2026, *Improved Rate for Non-Malleable Codes and Time-Lock Puzzles*.

title: Interoperable threshold protocol failure semantics
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Standardize and test how independent implementations handle malformed shares, complaints, aborts, refreshes, and participant replacement without divergent security interpretations.
status: NIST’s 2026 threshold initiative is active; a complete interoperable suite is not implied by a call for schemes.
why: Threshold security depends on agreement about failure behavior.
key_works: NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography*, NISTIR 8214C.

title: Bias-resistant randomness beacons under committee churn
subfield: Signatures, threshold cryptography, and delay functions
open: Deliver public randomness with quantified bias, availability, and recovery guarantees while a large committee changes membership and some members selectively abort.
status: Proposed end-to-end target combining threshold generation, durable state, and adversarial scheduling.
why: Many decentralized protocols inherit any bias or downtime in their randomness source.
key_works: Boneh et al., 2018, *Verifiable Delay Functions*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography*.

title: Portable source-to-binary constant-time guarantees
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Prove that production compiler transformations preserve the intended constant-time property across supported architectures and optimization settings.
status: Verified libraries exist, but compiler-generated operations and architecture-specific timing remain important seams; KyberSlash illustrates one class of failure.
why: Source-level coding discipline is not a complete machine-code guarantee.
key_works: Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt*; Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*, ePrint 2024/1049.

title: Constant-time security under dynamic voltage and frequency scaling
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Develop enforceable leakage models and countermeasures that account for secret-dependent power affecting execution time through frequency scaling.
status: Hertzbleed demonstrated that constant instruction timing is not sufficient against this mechanism.
why: It challenges a central software-side-channel abstraction.
key_works: Wang, Paccagnella, He, Shacham, and Fletcher, 2022, *Hertzbleed: Turning Power Side-Channel Attacks into Remote Timing Attacks on x86*.

title: Scalable verification of high-order masked implementations
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Verify large masked circuits at higher orders with tractable time and memory while modeling relevant glitches and compositional interfaces.
status: Strong progress exists, but historical examples show verification cost growing sharply with order and circuit size.
why: Unverified masking complexity can become its own security risk.
key_works: Bloem, Iusupov, Krenn, and Mangard, 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling: Efficient Formal Verification of Higher-Order Masking*, ePrint 2018/1031.

title: Joint glitch, transition, and coupling leakage models
