subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Establish experimentally validated compositional models incorporating glitches, transitions, routing effects, and physical coupling without making verification unusably conservative.
status: Existing formal models capture important subsets of physical behavior; joint soundness remains a stronger target.
why: A proof in an incomplete leakage model can miss real leakage.
key_works: Bloem et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/1031; Barthe et al., 2016, *Strong Non-Interference and Type-Directed Higher-Order Masking*.

title: Masking-preserving compilation and layout
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Preserve high-order masking guarantees through compiler scheduling, register allocation, instruction selection, and hardware placement.
status: Component-level masking proofs do not automatically survive these transformations.
why: Backend optimization can reconnect shares that were separated in the design.
key_works: Bloem et al., 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling*; HACL*/Vale/EverCrypt project documentation.

title: Low-overhead higher-order masking of post-quantum signing
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Implement third-order-protected post-quantum signing with a declared low energy-overhead target and independent leakage validation across devices.
status: Proposed moonshot; first- and higher-order masking work exists for candidate schemes, but performance and assurance must be evaluated jointly.
why: Post-quantum migration must not abandon physical-attack resistance.
key_works: NIST, 2025, *mUOV: Masking the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar Digital Signature Scheme at First- and Higher-Order*; related physical-security presentations.

title: Composable security against combined faults and leakage
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Prove and experimentally validate implementations secure against a declared combination of fault injections and side-channel observations, including attacks that use one to amplify the other.
status: Separate fault and leakage countermeasures need not compose.
why: Real attackers can combine physical capabilities.
key_works: Bauer, 2025, *Fault Attacks against UOV-Based Signatures*; Bloem et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/1031.

title: Verified cryptography across foreign-function and serialization boundaries
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Extend implementation proofs through parsers, bindings, memory ownership, encodings, and error handling used by applications.
status: Verified cryptographic kernels are substantial progress, but they do not automatically verify every integration layer.
why: Many exploitable failures occur around rather than inside the mathematical primitive.
key_works: Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider*; HACL*/Vale/EverCrypt documentation.

title: Cross-device side-channel generalization benchmarks
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Build shared datasets spanning chips, manufacturing variation, aging, temperature, compilers, and measurement setups, with held-out devices for attack evaluation.
status: Proposed data target; same-device training and testing do not establish transferable attack or defense performance.
why: It would make physical-security claims less dependent on one laboratory setup.
key_works: Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*.

title: Statistical meaning of “no leakage detected”
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Derive useful confidence statements about leakage within explicit adversary and measurement classes, distinguishing failure to detect from evidence of bounded exploitability.
status: Proposed methodological target; finite experiments cannot certify absence of every conceivable side channel.
why: It would prevent negative test results from being overstated as security proofs.
key_works: Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; NIST, 2018, *Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation*, SP 800-90B.

title: Optimal randomness consumption for composable masking
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Determine tight fresh-randomness requirements for specified masking orders and circuit classes, with constructions that retain composability under the declared leakage model.
status: Randomness-efficient gadgets exist; global optimality across realistic composition constraints remains unresolved.
why: Fresh randomness can dominate masked implementation cost.
key_works: Bloem et al., 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling*, ePrint 2018/1031; Belaïd et al., 2018, *Tight Private Circuits* (full title verify), ePrint 2018/439.

title: Optimal bandwidth–healing tradeoffs for post-quantum ratchets
open: Determine the minimum communication needed to recover post-quantum secrecy after compromise under asynchronous, lossy messaging and explicit adversarial scheduling.
status: Signal’s Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet and Triple Ratchet mean basic post-quantum ratcheting is not the unresolved question.
why: Frequent healing must coexist with mobile bandwidth and intermittent connectivity.
key_works: Signal, living specification, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*, sections on SPQR and Triple Ratchet.

title: Multi-device post-quantum post-compromise security
open: Establish practical guarantees when compromise affects different devices at different times, including device linking, unlinking, state synchronization, and stale backups.
status: Proposed lifecycle target beyond a two-endpoint ratchet.
why: A recovered device should not be re-compromised by another device’s stale state.
key_works: Signal, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*; Barnes et al., 2023, *The Messaging Layer Security Protocol*, RFC 9420.

title: Efficient post-quantum group healing with long-offline members
open: Maintain authenticated group state and strong healing guarantees while accommodating long-offline members without unbounded update history or excessive reinitialization.
status: MLS provides a deployed protocol framework; post-quantum efficiency and offline-state handling remain parameter- and application-dependent.
why: Real groups contain intermittently connected devices.
key_works: Barnes et al., 2023, *The Messaging Layer Security Protocol*, RFC 9420.

title: Practical post-quantum deniability with explicit compromise semantics
open: Deliver efficient post-quantum messaging with a precisely defined deniability guarantee that survives the intended key-exposure and transcript-disclosure scenarios.
status: Authentication, forward secrecy, and deniability are different properties; adding a post-quantum KEM does not automatically establish all three.
why: Users and applications may rely on properties stronger than confidentiality.
key_works: Signal, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm* and its post-quantum extensions.

title: Secure backup restoration without resurrecting compromised epochs
open: Characterize and implement the minimum freshness assumptions needed to restore encrypted messaging state without reusing keys or silently undoing post-compromise recovery.
status: Proposed target; entirely rollbackable local state cannot by itself prove freshness.
why: Recovery features can reverse the security gains of ratcheting.
key_works: Signal, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*; Barnes et al., RFC 9420.

title: Low-latency messaging resistant to global traffic analysis
open: Determine and approach the privacy–latency–bandwidth frontier for interactive messaging against global observers, including realistic user activity and long-term correlation.
status: Systems such as Vuvuzela demonstrate strong possibilities with cover traffic; the tradeoff is not eliminated.
why: Encrypted content does not hide who communicates with whom.
key_works: van den Hooff, Lazar, Zaharia, and Zeldovich, 2015, *Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis*, DOI 10.1145/2815400.2815417.

title: Private, abuse-resistant contact discovery at global scale
open: Support very large, frequently updated contact directories while hiding queries, limiting enumeration, and retaining mobile-scale bandwidth without trusting a single privileged enclave.
status: Scalable private contact-discovery protocols exist; enumeration resistance and operational leakage are additional requirements.
why: Discovery can reveal a user’s social graph before messaging begins.
key_works: Kales, Rechberger, Schneider, Senker, and Weinert, 2019, *Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale*; accompanying implementation.

title: Low-cost post-quantum strong asymmetric PAKE
open: Match the deployment efficiency and strong server-compromise properties of mature asymmetric PAKE designs using post-quantum assumptions and explicit composable security.
status: Proposed practicality target. OPAQUE already addresses precomputation resistance; generic resistance to offline guessing after total server compromise is not assumed.
why: Password-based systems also need quantum migration.
key_works: Jarecki, Krawczyk, and Xu, 2018, *OPAQUE: An Asymmetric PAKE Protocol Secure Against Pre-Computation Attacks*, ePrint 2018/163.

title: Privacy-preserving global password-guess throttling
open: Prevent distributed online guessing without creating a global identity-tracking service, under explicit assumptions about Sybil resistance, server compromise, and recovery.
status: Proposed systems problem; cryptography alone cannot impose scarcity on unlimited unauthenticated identities.
why: Strong password protocols still need safe online-attempt limits.
key_works: Jarecki et al., 2018, *OPAQUE*, ePrint 2018/163; Canetti et al., 2012, *Efficient Password Authenticated Key Exchange via Oblivious Transfer*.

title: Private key transparency with global equivocation detection
open: Detect split views and malicious key changes while protecting lookup privacy, minimizing client monitoring, and supporting large-scale key rotation and account recovery.
status: CONIKS supplies a major baseline; its existence does not settle every privacy, recovery, and deployment tradeoff.
why: End-to-end encryption fails if users are silently given attacker-controlled keys.
key_works: Melara, Blankstein, Bonneau, Felten, and Freedman, 2015, *CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users*, ePrint 2014/1004.

title: Compact post-quantum anonymous credentials
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Achieve selective disclosure, unlinkable presentation, and malicious-issuer security with post-quantum assumptions and mobile-friendly proof sizes.
status: Proposed practical target; efficient pairing-based credentials establish a classical baseline, not quantum resistance.
why: Identity systems need privacy-preserving migration rather than simply larger signatures.

title: Revocation without presentation linkability
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Revoke credentials promptly while preventing revocation checks, witness updates, and issuer interactions from linking a holder’s presentations.
status: Accumulators and revocation mechanisms address portions of the problem; lifecycle metadata remains part of the target.
why: A privacy-preserving credential should remain private when it expires or is revoked.
key_works: Sonnino et al., *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Melara et al., *CONIKS*, ePrint 2014/1004.

title: Auditable threshold issuance without holder deanonymization
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Make distributed issuers accountable for unauthorized or inconsistent issuance while ensuring audit evidence does not identify honest holders or link presentations.
status: Threshold issuance already exists; public accountability under malicious behavior is a distinct proposed requirement.
why: Privacy should not require unaccountable credential authorities.
key_works: Sonnino et al., 2018–2019, *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344.

title: Minimal assumptions for privacy-preserving credential nontransferability
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Characterize which nontransferability guarantees are possible when a willing holder cooperates with a buyer, and what hardware, interaction, or external assumptions are indispensable.
status: Proposed classification problem; ordinary software secrets can be copied, so unconditional nontransferability is not presumed.
why: It would separate attainable holder binding from misleading claims.
key_works: Sonnino et al., *Coconut*; Aaronson, 2009, *Quantum Copy-Protection and Quantum Money*.

title: Anonymous rate limits without universal tracking identifiers
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Enforce per-holder limits across a federation while preventing issuers and verifiers from reconstructing cross-service behavior.
status: Proposed target with explicit enrollment and Sybil assumptions; anonymity does not itself solve unique-human enrollment.
why: Many useful anonymous services otherwise collapse under abuse.
key_works: Sonnino et al., *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Kales et al., 2019, *Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale*.

title: Tight assumptions for remote coercion resistance
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Characterize the weakest private-channel, honest-device, or unobserved-interaction assumptions sufficient for remote voting coercion resistance under explicit coercer capabilities.
status: Coercion-resistant protocols exist under assumptions; complete surveillance cannot simply be wished away.
why: It would make election-security claims precise about their unavoidable trust requirements.
key_works: Juels, Catalano, and Jakobsson, 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*, ePrint 2002/165; DOI 10.1145/1102199.1102213.

title: Large-scale coercion-resistant revoting with practical tallying
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Demonstrate coercion-resistant revoting for a declared ten-million-ballot workload with publicly verifiable tallying, bounded memory, and robust handling of malicious submissions.
status: Proposed scaling target; deniable revoting constructions exist, but benchmark assumptions and tally costs matter.
why: Stronger voting guarantees must survive realistic election scale.
key_works: Achenbach et al., 2015, *Improved Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections through Deniable Re-Voting*.

title: Human-verifiable coercion resistance under realistic error
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Demonstrate that ordinary users can carry out the security-critical steps of a coercion-resistant protocol despite mistakes, accessibility needs, and deceptive instructions.
status: Proposed experimental target; a formal protocol proof does not establish usable human behavior.
why: Security that depends on reliably performed human actions needs direct evidence.
key_works: Juels–Catalano–Jakobsson, 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*; Achenbach et al., 2015, *Deniable Re-Voting*.

title: Practical post-quantum coercion-resistant election proofs
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Combine post-quantum ballot privacy, coercion resistance, and universally verifiable tallying with practical proof sizes and explicit long-term archival guarantees.
status: Proposed joint target; substituting a KEM or signature does not establish the whole election protocol’s security.
why: Ballot secrecy and audit records can need protection for decades.
key_works: Juels et al., 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*; Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046.

title: Complete-liability proofs without a trusted completeness oracle
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Characterize what external evidence is necessary for a private solvency proof to establish that all liabilities were included, rather than merely checking arithmetic over a chosen subset.
status: Proofs of assets and committed liabilities exist; cryptography cannot automatically discover undisclosed obligations.
why: It would clarify the boundary between cryptographic verification and real-world accounting truth.
key_works: Dagher, Bünz, Bonneau, Clark, and Boneh, 2015, *Provisions: Privacy-Preserving Proofs of Solvency for Bitcoin Exchanges*, ePrint 2015/1008.

title: General two-party secret-key capacity
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Determine the exact asymptotic secret-key rate obtainable from an arbitrary finite joint distribution of two honest parties’ observations and an eavesdropper’s information.
status: General lower and upper bounds exist; the July 2026 existence result for bipartite bound information does not supply a complete capacity formula.
why: It would characterize the secrecy inherently present in correlated data.
key_works: Maurer, 1993, DOI 10.1109/18.256484; Maurer–Wolf, 1999, *Intrinsic Conditional Information*; Pauwels–Gisin–Renner, 2026, arXiv:2607.25838.

title: Deciding positive distillable secrecy
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Give a general effective criterion for whether a finite rational distribution has positive two-party distillable secret key under unrestricted public discussion.
status: Bound information now exists, so positive secrecy-formation cost alone cannot be used as the criterion.
why: A decision criterion would separate useful correlations from nondistillable secrecy.
key_works: Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838.

title: Activation and compositional structure of bound information
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Characterize when nondistillable secret correlations become useful when combined with other correlations, including whether sharp activation criteria exist.
status: The 2026 existence theorem opens a concrete bipartite setting for questions beyond existence.
why: It would reveal whether apparently unusable secrecy can become a composable resource.
key_works: Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838; Maurer–Wolf, 1999.

title: Online entropy certification under drift
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Certify a conservative usable entropy rate when physical noise sources drift, age, or undergo environmental changes, without assuming stationary behavior that testing cannot justify.
status: Standards provide assessment procedures; robust nonstationary certification is a stronger proposed target.
why: Randomness failures can invalidate otherwise correct cryptography.
key_works: NIST, 2018, *Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation*, SP 800-90B.

title: Entropy combiners robust to correlated source failures
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Determine optimal extraction guarantees when several physical sources may fail or become correlated, stating exactly what independence or conditional-entropy assumptions are necessary.
status: Proposed classification and implementation target; combining two weak sources does not automatically produce strong randomness.
why: Redundant randomness hardware is useful only under defensible failure assumptions.
key_works: NIST, 2018, SP 800-90B; Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, arXiv:cs/0602007.

title: Reusable fuzzy extraction under correlated enrollment
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Reuse noisy biometric or physical measurements across services and enrollments without cumulative helper-data leakage exceeding a precisely bounded budget.
status: Fuzzy extraction exists; correlated reuse and realistic auxiliary information are additional requirements.
why: A biometric cannot simply be replaced after every disclosure.
key_works: Dodis, Ostrovsky, Reyzin, and Smith, 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors: How to Generate Strong Keys from Biometrics and Other Noisy Data*, DOI 10.1137/060651380.

title: Optimal fuzzy extraction for edit-like metrics
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Obtain near-optimal entropy loss and efficient reconstruction for realistic insertion, deletion, and alignment errors under adversarial helper-data manipulation.
status: General frameworks and constructions exist; optimality depends strongly on the error metric and robustness requirements.
why: Hamming-distance models do not capture every noisy physical or biometric source.
key_works: Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, arXiv:cs/0602007.

title: Realistic conditional biometric-entropy datasets
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Build consented, representative datasets enabling conservative estimates of biometric entropy conditioned on population information, related measurements, and previously released helper data.
status: Proposed data target; nominal sensor resolution is not a measure of extractable secret entropy.
why: Cryptographic biometric claims require defensible source models.
key_works: Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, ePrint 2003/235; NIST SP 800-90B.

title: Steganography under channel-model misspecification
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Maintain quantified undetectability when the encoder’s channel model differs from the observer’s real distribution and changes over time.
status: Provably secure constructions depend on explicit channel or sampling assumptions; those assumptions need not hold exactly in natural data.
why: Distribution mismatch can overwhelm a theoretically secure embedding method.
key_works: Hopper, Langford, and von Ahn, 2002, *Provably Secure Steganography*, ePrint 2002/137; Liao et al., 2025, *A Framework for Designing Provably Secure Steganography*.

title: Robust steganographic capacity under common transformations
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Determine achievable hidden-message rates under a declared family of compression, resizing, editing, and re-encoding operations while preserving undetectability.
status: Particular robust constructions exist; they do not establish a general capacity frontier.
why: Real communication channels transform content.
key_works: Wang et al., 2025, *SparSamp: Efficient Provably Secure Steganography Based on Sparse Sampling*, arXiv:2503.19499; Qi et al., 2025, robust-image steganography work.

title: Interactive generative steganography with composable guarantees
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Preserve undetectability over long adaptive conversations while controlling latency, sampling cost, semantic quality, and recovery from message loss.
status: Proposed systems target; single-message distribution preservation is not a complete interactive security argument.
why: Interactive generative channels introduce state and feedback absent from static examples.
key_works: Ding et al., 2023, *Discop: Provably Secure Steganography in Practice Based on “Distribution Copies”*; Wang et al., 2025, *SparSamp*.

title: Explicit two-split-state non-malleable codes approaching capacity
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Construct efficient information-theoretic two-split-state non-malleable codes with rate approaching \(1/2\) and negligible error.
status: Capacity \(1/2\) is known; explicit rate-one-third constructions are an important milestone. Computational and extra-state results are different settings.
why: It would close a major explicit-construction gap in tamper resistance.
key_works: Cheraghchi–Guruswami, 2013–2014, *Capacity of Non-Malleable Codes*, arXiv:1309.0458; Aggarwal et al., 2022, *Rate One-Third Non-malleable Codes*.

title: Public-key quantum money from plain LWE in the standard model
open: Construct publicly verifiable quantum money from plain LWE with standard-model security, without generic-group-action or ideal-oracle qualifications.
status: Generic-model constructions from standard assumptions are substantial progress but do not settle this target.
why: It would ground reusable quantum tokens in a widely studied assumption.
key_works: Doliskani, 2025–2026, *Public-Key Quantum Money from Standard Assumptions (In the Generic Model)*, ePrint 2025/092.

title: Quantum lightning from conservative standard-model assumptions
open: Construct quantum lightning with publicly verifiable uniqueness from independently credible post-quantum assumptions, without relying on an idealized model or fragile special-purpose assumption.
status: Candidate and generic-model approaches exist; quantum money and lightning have different security requirements.
why: Lightning would enable uniquely identifiable quantum objects without centralized issuance.
key_works: Zhandry, 2017–2019, *Quantum Lightning Never Strikes the Same State Twice*, arXiv:1711.02276; Zhandry, 2023–2025, *Quantum Money from Abelian Group Actions*, arXiv:2307.12120.

title: Reusable quantum-token experiments with meaningful security evidence
open: Demonstrate repeated verification and storage of a quantum token while quantifying honest rejection, degradation, and the security model against counterfeiting.
status: Proposed experimental target; observing no-cloning-related behavior alone is not a cryptographic security demonstration.
why: Practical tokens need both durability and a defensible adversary model.
key_works: Aaronson and Christiano, 2012, *Quantum Money from Hidden Subspaces*, arXiv:1203.4740; Zhandry, *Quantum Lightning*.

title: Characterizing quantum-copy-protectable function classes
open: Give useful necessary and sufficient conditions for efficiently copy-protecting function families, beyond the observation that efficiently learnable functions cannot be protected.
status: Positive results cover important restricted classes; unrestricted classification remains a different problem.
why: It would identify which software functionality can fundamentally benefit from quantum protection.
key_works: Aaronson, 2009, *Quantum Copy-Protection and Quantum Money*; Coladangelo, Majenz, and Poremba, 2024, DOI 10.22331/q-2024-05-02-1330.

title: Broad copy protection without indistinguishability obfuscation
open: Protect broad classes such as suitable puncturable cryptographic functions from plain LWE or similarly conservative assumptions without assuming quantum-secure iO.
status: The 2025 revisited framework obtains strong results from quantum-secure iO plus LWE; removing iO is the sharper target.
why: It would substantially simplify the foundations of unclonable software.
key_works: Ananth, Behera, Huang, Kitagawa, and Yamakawa, 2025, *Copy-Protection from Unclonable Puncturable Obfuscation, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/1880.

title: Standard-model quantum-state obfuscation for useful restricted classes
open: Replace classical-oracle idealizations in quantum-state obfuscation by explicit constructions for useful restricted program classes under stated assumptions.
status: Oracle-model results for pseudodeterministic classical-input/output computation do not establish unrestricted standard-model obfuscation.
why: It would turn a powerful idealized primitive into a concrete one.
key_works: Bartusek, Brakerski, and Vaikuntanathan, 2024, *Quantum State Obfuscation from Classical Oracles*, arXiv:2401.10200.

title: Composition of strong unclonability definitions
open: Determine which unclonable-encryption guarantees survive adaptive multi-instance use, entangled side information, and later key revelation, with tight implications or separations between definitions.
status: One-out-of-many constructions exist; their existence does not establish every stronger composition property.
why: Real applications use many correlated tokens or ciphertexts rather than one isolated challenge.
key_works: *One-out-of-Many Unclonable Cryptography: Definitions, Constructions, and More*, 2023–2026, arXiv:2302.09836; authors verify.

title: Long-distance field device-independent QKD
open: Demonstrate positive finite-key device-independent secret-key generation over a declared long-distance field link without fair-sampling assumptions or hidden trusted measurement-device models.
status: Bell-certified experimental QKD was demonstrated in 2022; long-distance field operation is a stronger target.
why: It would move device-independent security toward deployable communication.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*, DOI 10.1038/s41586-022-04941-5.

title: Useful device-independent key rates under realistic noise
open: Achieve sustained application-useful finite-key rates while accounting for detection inefficiency, memory noise, drift, and non-independent device behavior.
status: Proposed scaling target; asymptotic positive rates and idealized noise thresholds are insufficient.
why: A secure bit generated extremely slowly may not support practical services.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*; Anwer et al., 2026, *Experimental Quantum Randomness Generation and Key Distribution with Entangled Photons*.

title: Safe reuse of device-independent cryptographic hardware
open: Establish enforceable composable guarantees for reused devices with internal memory, including allowed inter-session communication and mechanisms preventing past-secret leakage.
status: Device independence does not mean independence from every isolation and information-flow assumption.
why: Devices are normally reused, making cross-session memory behavior security-critical.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*.

title: Exact secret-key capacity of thermal-loss channels
open: Determine the exact two-way assisted secret-key capacity of general bosonic thermal-loss channels by matching achievable rates with upper bounds.
status: The pure-loss repeaterless capacity is known; nonzero thermal noise leaves broader unresolved regimes.
why: It would establish fundamental limits for realistic optical communication.
key_works: Pirandola, Laurenza, Ottaviani, and Banchi, 2017, *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, DOI 10.1038/ncomms15043.

title: Secure memory-based repeater advantage in a complete field system
open: Demonstrate an end-to-end, finite-key-secure memory-based repeater chain exceeding the appropriate point-to-point benchmark while reporting all elementary-link and memory resources.
status: Proposed experimental target; changing the network model does not “violate” a repeaterless bound.
why: It would validate the practical value of quantum repeaters for cryptographic communication.
key_works: Pirandola et al., 2017, *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, arXiv:1510.08863.

title: Whole-system QKD security including endpoints
open: Demonstrate a composable security account covering authentication, random-number generation, classical processing, key storage, control software, and physical leakage alongside the optical protocol.
status: Proposed assurance target; a quantum-channel proof does not verify every endpoint component.
why: Endpoints can compromise keys without defeating quantum mechanics.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*; NIST SP 800-90B.

title: Certified quantum randomness per joule under drift
open: Improve certified random-bit production per joule tenfold against a pinned complete-system baseline while maintaining finite-size guarantees under realistic drift.
status: Proposed moonshot; raw detection rate is not the same as certified extractable randomness.
why: It would make strong randomness generation more economical and portable.
key_works: Anwer, Mahammedi, Muhammad, Mironowicz, and Bourennane, 2026, *Experimental Quantum Randomness Generation and Key Distribution with Entangled Photons*, DOI 10.1103/x13g-h5xm.

title: Tight fairness–latency–resilience frontiers for transaction ordering
subfield: Decentralized protocols and cryptographic economic systems
open: Characterize achievable ordering fairness under explicit network timing, Byzantine fraction, and latency requirements, including matching impossibility results.
status: Aequitas introduced formal order-fairness constructions; fairness is not simply equivalent to consensus consistency and liveness.
why: Adversarial ordering can create economic harm even when consensus is correct.
key_works: Kelkar, Zhang, Goldfeder, and Juels, 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*, ePrint 2020/269.

title: Encrypted transaction ordering with robust release
subfield: Decentralized protocols and cryptographic economic systems
open: Hide transaction contents until order commitment while guaranteeing threshold decryption or a precisely specified safe fallback under withholding, churn, and network partitions.
status: Proposed integration target; encrypted submission alone does not solve decryption availability or censorship.
why: Content privacy is useful only if adversaries cannot exploit selective release.
key_works: Kelkar et al., 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography*.

title: Verifiable ordering guarantees with explicit economic meaning
subfield: Decentralized protocols and cryptographic economic systems
open: Connect formal ordering properties to bounded adversarial economic advantage under congestion and strategic submission, rather than assuming that one fairness definition eliminates all extractable value.
status: Proposed theory target; order fairness and economic fairness are not identical notions.
why: It would make cryptographic ordering guarantees meaningful for actual applications.
key_works: Kelkar et al., 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*; Kelkar et al., 2023, *Themis: Fast, Strong Order-Fairness in Byzantine Consensus*.

title: Ground-truth cryptographic-inventory benchmarks
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Build representative benchmark environments with complete ground truth for cryptography hidden in binaries, libraries, protocols, certificates, hardware, and archived data.
status: Proposed data target aligned with current post-quantum discovery work; scanner output alone cannot establish recall.
why: Organizations cannot migrate cryptography they cannot find.
key_works: NIST NCCoE, ongoing *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*, discovery and interoperability workstreams.

title: Downgrade-safe hybrid migration under real failures
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Demonstrate interoperable hybrid cryptographic migration that preserves its security claims across retries, partial upgrades, fallback, middleboxes, and restored configurations.
status: Proposed deployment target; supporting two algorithms does not automatically yield a secure hybrid protocol.
why: Migration failures can silently restore the weaker security level.
key_works: NIST NCCoE, *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*, interoperability workstream and SP 1800-38 drafts.

title: Long-lived signed archives through repeated algorithm replacement
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Preserve verifiable provenance across multiple cryptographic deprecations, key losses, and archival migrations without retroactively trusting evidence created after compromise.
status: Proposed lifecycle target; replacing a signature algorithm today does not automatically preserve decades-old evidence.
why: Scientific, governmental, and commercial records may outlive every initial algorithm.
key_works: NIST NCCoE, *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*; NIST, *Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization*.

title: Common resource accounting for cryptanalytic estimates
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Publish comparable attack-cost records including operations, memory capacity and traffic, parallelism, energy, success probability, and quantum error-correction assumptions.
status: Proposed benchmark target; “bits of security” can conceal materially different cost models.
why: Comparable evidence is necessary to compare cryptographic families fairly.
key_works: Chen et al., 2020, *On the Concrete Security of LWE with Small Secret*; Kachigar–Tillich, 2017, *Quantum Information Set Decoding Algorithms*.

title: Publishable negative cryptanalysis and independent replication
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Create a maintained repository of unsuccessful attack searches with code, parameter coverage, compute budgets, stopping rules, and independently reproduced positive controls.
status: Proposed infrastructure gap; failure to find an attack is useful only when the search and its limitations are inspectable.
why: It would reduce duplicated effort and improve confidence calibration.
key_works: Gohr, 2019, *Improving Attacks on Round-Reduced Speck32/64 Using Deep Learning*, accompanying code; Chen et al., 2020, ePrint 2020/539.

title: Sustainable maintenance funding for critical cryptographic libraries
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Identify and test funding mechanisms that sustain security maintenance, independent review, incident response, and succession for widely depended-on cryptographic libraries.
status: Proposed funding research target; general open-source surveys provide a baseline, not proof that every cryptographic project has the same constraint.
why: Correct cryptography can become unsafe when its maintenance fails.
key_works: Nagle, Wheeler, Lifshitz-Assaf, Ham, and Hoffman, 2020, *Report on the 2020 FOSS Contributor Survey*.

title: Shared independent physical-security laboratories
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Establish sustainable shared access to equipment, expertise, and reproducible testing for fault and side-channel evaluation, with measured effects on coverage and independent replication.
status: Proposed funding target; its success criterion is increased independent assurance, not merely purchasing equipment.
why: Expensive testing infrastructure can limit scrutiny of deployed cryptography.
key_works: Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*; Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; Nagle et al., 2020, *FOSS Contributor Survey*.

title: Funding proof maintenance after verification milestones
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Develop and evaluate funding models that keep formal proofs synchronized with evolving compilers, architectures, APIs, and optimized implementations.
status: Proposed funding target; a one-time verification result is not a permanent maintenance mechanism.
why: Assurance can decay while the software continues to ship.
key_works: Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt*; MIT, 2022, *High-Assurance Cryptography* project; Nagle et al., 2020, *FOSS Contributor Survey*.

title: A versioned, evidence-linked cryptographic open-problem registry
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Build a registry representing precise statements, assumptions, parameter regimes, equivalences, partial results, refutations, and resolution dates, with human-auditable source links.
status: Proposed data-infrastructure target. The 2026 secret-sharing and bound-information resolutions illustrate why static “open problem” lists become incorrect.
why: It would make a large cross-linked census searchable, maintainable, and resistant to duplicated or obsolete entries.
key_works: Nir, 2026, ECCC TR26-146; Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838.

title: R11.01. Helleseth’s vanishing conjecture beyond established exponent families
open: Prove that, whenever \(q>2\) and \(d\equiv1\pmod{p-1}\), some nonzero \(a\) satisfies \(W_{F,d}(a)=0\), or produce a counterexample.
status: Proposed in 1971. Niho exponents are settled in every characteristic; the unrestricted conjecture remains unresolved in the reviewed literature.
why: It would establish a universal spectral constraint rather than another family-specific calculation.
key_works: Liem Nguyen, 2020/2022, *On Weil Sums, Conjectures of Helleseth, and Niho Exponents*, arXiv:2006.15726, Conjecture 1.2.
aliases: Helleseth vanishing conjecture; singularity conjecture for power permutations.

title: R11.02. Helleseth’s three-valued conjecture in characteristic at least five
open: For \(F=\mathbb F_{p^n}\) with \(n\) a power of two, prove that an invertible exponent cannot have an exactly three-valued Weil spectrum when \(p\ge5\).
status: The conjecture dates to 1971. Characteristics two and three are proved; those results do not settle the remaining characteristics.
why: It would exclude an entire class of exceptionally sparse correlation spectra.
key_works: Daniel J. Katz, 2018, *Weil Sums of Binomials: Properties, Applications, and Open Problems*, arXiv:1805.10452, Conjecture 10.6.

title: R11.03. Symmetry of every three-valued Weil spectrum
open: Prove that every three-valued spectrum of an invertible power function has the form \(\{0,A,-A\}\), or exhibit an asymmetric example.
status: Integrality, the occurrence of zero, and opposite signs of the other values are established. Equality of their magnitudes remains the stronger conjecture.
why: It would turn several separate spectral restrictions into a rigid classification principle.
key_works: Katz, 2018, *Weil Sums of Binomials: Properties, Applications, and Open Problems*, arXiv:1805.10452, Conjecture 10.5.

title: R11.04. Nguyen’s five-valued Niho conjecture outside the small-\(k\) window
open: Let \(q=p^n\), \(p\) odd, and \(d=1+k(q-1)\) be a nondegenerate invertible Niho exponent over \(\mathbb F_{q^2}\). Prove that \(\gcd(k,q+1)+\gcd(k-1,q+1)\ge5\) forces at least five spectral values.
status: Nguyen proves the claim for \(n\ge2\) and \(2\le k<p/2+1\), with another restricted result for \(n=1\). The unrestricted range remains.
why: It would resolve a concrete boundary between low-valued and richer spectra.
key_works: Nguyen, *On Weil Sums, Conjectures of Helleseth, and Niho Exponents*, arXiv:2006.15726, Conjecture 1.7 and Theorem 1.10.

title: R11.05. Divisibility of the product of distinct nonzero spectral values
open: Characterize exponents for which \(q\) divides the product of the **distinct nonzero** values of \(W_{F,d}\), initially restricting to integral spectra.
status: Explicit Problem 3.7 in Katz–Langevin. Fourier identities motivate the question but do not establish the divisibility generally.
why: This could supply new arithmetic obstructions to proposed spectra.
key_works: Daniel J. Katz and Philippe Langevin, 2014/2015, *New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth*, arXiv:1412.8530.

title: R11.06. A four-valued analogue of Katz’s spectral-structure theorem
open: Determine which integrality, zero-occurrence, and exponent-congruence restrictions survive when a power permutation has exactly four spectral values.
status: Explicit Problem 3.6 in Katz–Langevin; no general resolution was located. Their three-valued theorem does not automatically extend.
why: It would organize four-valued examples by structural necessity rather than construction alone.
key_works: Katz and Langevin, 2014/2015, *New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth*, arXiv:1412.8530.

title: R11.07. The optimal resilience of two-round full-information coin flipping
open: Determine the largest adversarial coalition tolerable by two-round collective coin-flipping protocols when each participant broadcasts one bit per round.
status: The 2025 bounds leave a gap between constructions tolerating roughly \(n/[\log n\,\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)]\) corruptions and attacks using \(O(n/\log\log n)\).
why: This isolates the value of one additional interaction round.
key_works: Eshan Chattopadhyay, Mohit Gurumukhani, Noam Ringach, and Rocco Servedio, 2025, *Lower Bounds for Leader Election and Collective Coin Flipping, Revisited*, arXiv:2504.01856, §7.

title: R11.08. Simultaneously biasing polynomially many Boolean outputs
open: For every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{n^{0.01}}\), can one coalition of \(O(n/\log n)\) coordinates, using **one common strategy**, force each of \(0.01n^{0.01}\) selected output bits toward a chosen value with probability at least \(0.99\)?
status: Explicit Question 7.1 in the 2025 paper. Allowing different adversarial behavior for different outputs gives a weaker, established result.
why: A positive answer would sharpen the preceding coin-flipping lower bounds.
key_works: Chattopadhyay et al., 2025, *Lower Bounds for Leader Election and Collective Coin Flipping, Revisited*, arXiv:2504.01856.

title: R11.09. Perfectly fair leader election beyond commit-and-reveal lower bounds
open: Determine whether the logarithmic-round barrier for perfect game-theoretic fairness extends beyond commit-and-reveal-style protocols. In particular, preserve each honest participant’s election probability of at least \(1/n\) against \(n^\varepsilon\)-sized coalitions, using the same abort and fairness definitions.
status: The TCC 2024 work proves an \(\Omega(\log n)\) lower bound for the restricted protocol class. Sublogarithmic protocols with both approximate fairness and weaker coalition requirements do not answer this question.
why: It would distinguish a fundamental fairness barrier from a limitation of a familiar protocol architecture.
key_works: Ohad Klein, Ilan Komargodski, and Chenzhi Zhu, 2024/2025, *On the (Im)possibility of Game-Theoretically Fair Leader Election Protocols*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-78011-0_13.

title: R11.10. Vanishing-bias quantum weak coin flipping in constant quantum space
open: Construct ordinary, zero-penalty quantum weak coin-flipping protocols with arbitrarily small bias while keeping the number of qubits bounded independently of the bias; alternatively, prove space must grow.
status: Arbitrarily small bias is achievable, but the cited constructions require growing space. The 2025 penalty-based approach does not settle the zero-penalty case.
why: This separates communication-round complexity from quantum-memory requirements.
key_works: Atul Singh Arora, Carl A. Miller, Mauro E. S. Morales, and Jamie Sikora, 2025, *Cheat-Penalised Quantum Weak Coin-Flipping*, arXiv:2510.03218.

title: R11.11. A rigorous constant-space family for finite-penalty quantum coin flipping
open: For a fixed finite cheating penalty, prove a constant-qubit protocol family whose maximum dishonest expected payoff approaches \(1/2\). A concrete target is 24 qubits with penalty \(\Lambda=0.01\).
status: The 2025 paper supplies low-bias numerical constructions and evidence for arbitrarily small bias; finite examples are not a proof for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
why: It would turn numerical point-game evidence into an asymptotic resource theorem.
key_works: Arora, Miller, Morales, and Sikora, 2025, *Cheat-Penalised Quantum Weak Coin-Flipping*, arXiv:2510.03218.

title: R11.12. Closing the \(N^{2.5}\)-versus-\(N^3\) memory-hardness reduction gap
open: Strengthen the parallel-random-oracle analysis of the Blocki–Holman construction so that avoiding linear sustained space incurs cumulative memory complexity approaching \(N^3\), matching its dynamic-pebbling guarantee.
status: The 2026 treatment obtains a roughly \(N^{3-\varepsilon}\) alternative in the pebbling model but only \(N^{2.5-\varepsilon}\) in the parallel random-oracle model. The disjunction with sustained-space hardness is essential.
why: It would show whether the exponent loss reflects the reduction or a genuine attack opportunity.
key_works: Jeremiah Blocki and Blake Holman, 2025–2026, *Data-Dependent Memory-Hard Functions: Sustained Space and Cumulative Complexity Trade-offs in the Parallel Random Oracle Model*, arXiv:2508.06795; ePrint 2026/1724.

title: R11.13. Repairing the near-linear sustained-space conjecture for Argon2id
open: Prove a valid near-linear-space tradeoff for the analyzed Argon2id graph: for example, an adversary must retain \(\Omega(N^{0.99})\) words for \(\Omega(N)\) steps or incur superquadratic cumulative memory cost, under an explicit resource model.
status: An April 2026 correction withdrew a lemma and dependent results from the earlier analysis. The later partial regime with sustained-space exponent below \(5/6\) does not establish the near-linear target.
why: It would restore—or precisely delimit—a practically relevant hardness claim after a proof failure.
key_works: Blocki and Holman, *Sustained Space and Cumulative Complexity Trade-offs for Data-Dependent Memory-Hard Functions*, ePrint 2022/832, correction dated 13 April 2026; subsequent arXiv:2508.06795.

title: R11.14. Joint bandwidth hardness across three or more memory levels
open: Determine attainable and unavoidable traffic tradeoffs across a hierarchy of cache, main memory, and external memory when an adversary may recompute values. The target is a **joint** lower bound, not separate two-level bounds that cannot necessarily be attained simultaneously.
status: Proposed extension of established bandwidth-hardness frameworks. The 2024 work resolves important two-level questions, including the old scrypt bandwidth question; those are excluded here.
why: It would reveal whether an implementation saves cost or merely moves it between memory levels.
key_works: Jeremiah Blocki, Peiyuan Liu, Ling Ren, and Samson Zhou, 2024, *Bandwidth-Hard Functions: Reductions and Lower Bounds*, ePrint 2018/221; DOI:10.1007/s00145-024-09497-3.

title: R11.15. The 128-bit mutual-correlated-agreement radius
open: For the Reed–Solomon code families and rates specified by the Proximity Prize, determine the largest decoding radius \(\delta_C\) for which the mutual-correlated-agreement error satisfies \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{MCA}}(C,\delta_C)\le2^{-128}\), with explicit finite-parameter bounds.
status: A live concrete challenge, not merely an asymptotic capacity question. Both stronger bounds and matching counterexamples can advance it.
why: Better constants directly affect proof-system soundness and usable code rates.
key_works: Gal Arnon, Dan Boneh, and Giacomo Fenzi, 2026, *Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*, ePrint 2026/680; official Proximity Prize problem statements.
prize: Eligible under the **shared $1 million Proximity Prize pool**, not a separate $1 million award for this problem; announced deadline 31 December 2027, subject to the published rules.

title: R11.16. Concrete interleaved-list bounds at the \(2^{-128}|F|\) threshold
open: For the specified interleaved Reed–Solomon families, determine the largest radius at which the worst-case list size is at most \(2^{-128}|F|\), with explicit dependence on field size, rate, and interleaving depth.
status: Listed separately from mutual correlated agreement in the prize framework. An asymptotic polynomial list-size statement does not supply the required concrete inequality.
why: It would reduce conservative soundness losses caused by poorly quantified list sizes.
key_works: Arnon, Boneh, and Fenzi, 2026, *Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*, ePrint 2026/680; Proximity Prize grand challenges.
prize: Eligible under the same shared Proximity Prize pool.

title: R11.17. Closing the machine-checked koalaIRS12 soundness interval
open: Narrow the gap between proved soundness and explicit attacks for the fixed **koalaIRS12** benchmark, with contributions checked by its Lean formalization. Determine the optimum within the pinned model, rather than changing the protocol or threat model.
status: On 6 October 2026, the challenge reports an interval of **68.15 to 116.13 security bits**. The upper endpoint already excludes a 128-bit claim for this benchmark.
why: It provides a measurable target where either a stronger proof or a better attack is valuable.
key_works: Ethereum Foundation Formal Verification Team, 2026, *Raising Machine-Checked Security Benchmarks to Advance Hash-Based SNARKs through Agentic Collaboration*; the live better.codes benchmark and accepted certificates.

title: R11.18. Capacity-level ordinary Reed–Solomon decoding in small characteristic
open: Establish a capacity-level list-decoding theorem for ordinary Reed–Solomon codes over small-characteristic extension fields, with explicit hypotheses on evaluation domains—or identify the structural obstructions preventing such a theorem.
status: Jeronimo’s September 2026 preprint treats prime fields and extensions subject to characteristic restrictions. It does not establish the unrestricted small-characteristic counterpart.
why: It would connect new decoding results to fields attractive for cryptographic arithmetic.
key_works: Fernando Granha Jeronimo, 2026, *Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*, arXiv:2609.05870.

title: R11.19. Bit-polynomial-time decoding behind the new capacity theorem
open: For fixed slack from capacity, replace the new decoder’s \(q^{O_\gamma(1)}\) dependence by running time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log q\), while retaining its decoding radius and complete output list.
status: The September 2026 preprint gives polynomial dependence on field cardinality, not its bit length. This distinction matters when \(q\) is very large.
why: It separates an algorithmic existence theorem from scalability over cryptographic-size fields.
key_works: Jeronimo, 2026, *Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*, arXiv:2609.05870.

title: R11.20. Constant-rate worst-case two-split-state codes for quantum messages
open: Construct constant-rate non-malleable encodings of arbitrary quantum messages against two independently acting tamperers who may share entanglement, with negligible error and protection of external reference entanglement.
status: The cited work achieves weaker worst-case rate and stronger average-case results. Average-case constant rate does not settle arbitrary-message security.
why: It would remove a major efficiency gap in quantum tamper resistance.
key_works: Naresh Goud Boddu, Vipul Goyal, Rahul Jain, and João Ribeiro, 2023/2024, *Split-State Non-Malleable Codes and Secret Sharing Schemes for Quantum Messages*, arXiv:2308.06466, §1.4.

title: R11.21. The missing two-out-of-three quantum non-malleable threshold scheme
open: Construct non-malleable quantum secret sharing in which any two of three shares reconstruct, one share reveals nothing, and the declared split-state tampering guarantee holds.
status: The cited construction covers the other no-cloning-compatible threshold regimes but explicitly leaves the two-out-of-three case unresolved.
why: This is the smallest threshold configuration combining useful redundancy with quantum reconstruction.
key_works: Boddu, Goyal, Jain, and Ribeiro, *Split-State Non-Malleable Codes and Secret Sharing Schemes for Quantum Messages*, arXiv:2308.06466, open problems.

title: R11.22. Hardware-free stateful leakage resilience against NC¹
open: Eliminate trusted hardware from the stateful leakage-resilient-circuit setting studied by Wang, while retaining its bounded-complexity leakage guarantee; alternatively, prove a broader impossibility under the same model.
status: The July 2026 revision obtains a trusted component whose size is independent of the original circuit. It also blocks a proposed hardware-elimination route through the simultaneous requirements of perfect soundness and verifiable CRS generation; this does not exclude every alternative route.
why: It would determine whether the remaining trusted component is essential.
key_works: Yuyu Wang, 2025–2026, *Leakage-Resilient Circuits against NC¹, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/1463.

title: R11.23. Bidirectional ratcheting under continual leakage and full compromise
open: Extend leakage-resilient ratcheted key exchange to asynchronous bidirectional communication, combining bounded continual leakage with clearly specified recovery after full state compromise. State exactly which uncompromised updates and randomness assumptions permit recovery.
status: Collins–Colombo–Schaeffler’s 2025 construction is unidirectional and distinguishes sender and receiver leakage guarantees. Ordinary post-compromise security does not imply continual-leakage resilience.
why: It would close a model mismatch between interactive conversations and one-way leakage-resilient channels.
key_works: Daniel Collins, Simone Colombo, and Sina Schaeffler, 2025, *Towards Leakage-Resilient Ratcheted Key Exchange*, ePrint 2025/332; DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-91823-0_6.

title: R11.24. Are two fully protected calls necessary for an accordion mode?
open: Determine whether the Motte-and-Bailey leakage-resilient accordion framework can achieve its guarantee using only one fully protected tweakable-block-cipher call, or prove two necessary within an explicit construction class.
status: Proposed lower-bound frontier. The October 2026 revision gives constructions using two protected calls while allowing weaker protection elsewhere.
why: It would quantify the minimum expensive trusted computation.
key_works: Mario Marhuenda Beltrán and Mustafa Khairallah, 2026, *The Motte-and-Bailey Framework for Leakage-Resilient Accordion Modes: Featuring Qaitbay and Alicante*, ePrint 2026/122.

title: R11.25. Removing the ideal leakage-resilient PRG from accordion-mode proofs
open: Instantiate the framework’s idealized single-trace leakage-resilient generator with an explicit construction and sufficient composable guarantees, without merely assuming the entire desired leakage property.
status: Proposed assumption-reduction target. The current framework separates idealized generator security from its mode-level analysis; physical testing alone would not close this proof gap.
why: It would connect the mode theorem to a defensible concrete component.
key_works: Marhuenda Beltrán and Khairallah, 2026, *The Motte-and-Bailey Framework for Leakage-Resilient Accordion Modes*, ePrint 2026/122.

title: R11.26. Maliciously secure streaming function secret sharing
open: Secure reusable streaming function shares against malformed client ciphertexts, inconsistent function keys, and malicious server evaluations, while retaining local evaluation and compact persistent keys.
status: Explicit future work in the USENIX Security 2026 paper; the presented streaming protocols use semi-honest security assumptions.
why: A stream should not amplify one malformed input into persistent disclosure or corruption.
key_works: Xiangfu Song et al., 2026, *Streaming Function Secret Sharing and Its Applications*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: R11.27. General-predicate streaming FSS without special key-homomorphic PRFs
open: Obtain the paper’s general-predicate streaming functionality from ordinary PRFs and the underlying FSS primitive, avoiding its special key-homomorphic PRF requirement while preserving reusable compact keys.
status: The point-function compiler needs ordinary PRFs; the broader predicate construction uses a key-homomorphic PRF with a special zero-key property.
why: It could reduce both assumptions and the cost of broader streaming predicates.
key_works: Song et al., 2026, *Streaming Function Secret Sharing and Its Applications*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: R11.28. Plain-LWE receiver-non-committing IBE over an unrestricted identity space
open: Construct receiver-non-committing identity-based encryption from plain LWE for exponentially many possible identities, with polynomial-size public parameters and the full adaptive-exposure security required by the cited definition.
status: The February 2026 paper obtains DDH/LWE constructions for a polynomial-size identity space with compact public parameters. Its stronger pairing-based constructions do not remove this restriction under plain LWE.
why: It would support adaptive simulation without fixing a small universe of users in advance.
key_works: Rishab Goyal, Fuyuki Kitagawa, Venkata Koppula, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree, Ryo Nishimaki, and Takashi Yamakawa, 2026, *Non-Committing Attribute and Identity Based Encryption: Constructions and Applications*, author-hosted manuscript.

title: R11.29. Authority-secure watermarking with the simple extractable-PRG architecture
open: Recover security against a malicious watermarking authority while retaining the simpler extractable-PRG/GGM-style construction and comparable assumptions and efficiency; alternatively, establish a limitation of that architecture.
status: The 2024 construction deliberately forgoes security against the marking authority. Stronger authority-secure watermarking exists through different, more elaborate approaches; existence alone is therefore not the open problem.
why: It would avoid trusting the party responsible for attaching and tracing marks.
key_works: Estuardo Alpirez Bock, Chris Brzuska, and Russell W. F. Lai, 2024, *Simple Watermarking Pseudorandom Functions from Extractable Pseudorandom Generators*, DOI:10.62056/aevur-10k.

title: R11.30. A certified qubit–Toffoli frontier for elliptic-curve key recovery
open: Determine the attainable qubit-count versus Toffoli-count frontier for a pinned 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete-log circuit, explicitly distinguishing a standalone attack from amortization across many keys. Improve executable upper bounds or prove lower bounds for specified reversible-arithmetic subroutines.
status: Active optimization challenges exist, but an optimality certificate is a different objective from a better implementation. Litinski’s 2023 analysis includes important amortization and architecture choices; its headline count should not be treated as a universal current record.
why: It would make quantum threat estimates depend on reproducible circuit artifacts rather than incomparable resource headlines.
key_works: Daniel Litinski, 2023, *How to Compute a 256-Bit Elliptic Curve Private Key with Only 50 Million Toffoli Gates*, arXiv:2306.08585; the public ECDSA circuit-optimization challenge linked by ecdsa.fail.

title: Threshold signatures with full proactivity, identifiable aborts, and scale
open: Design a threshold signature scheme that simultaneously achieves: proactive secret refresh (periodic resharing with zero downtime), identifiable abort (who misbehaved, without extra rounds), adaptive security (corruption decided mid-protocol), threshold t of n with n >= 100 parties, and signing latency under ~200ms in a real WAN deployment. No known construction achieves all simultaneously; no published impossibility separates them either.
status: Constructions achieve pairs/triples: FROST/Sparkle-style threshold Schnorr (efficient, no proactivity), proactive schemes (refresh, slower), YOSO-style roles (adaptive, communication-heavy), identifying-abort MPC-in-the-head variants. The full combination is an open design envelope.
why: The blocking gap for threshold crypto in production key management (wallets, custody, CA keys, cross-chain bridges); each missing property is a real attack/incident class (insider denial, long-term key compromise, mobile adversaires).
key_works: Komlo–Goldsmith, "FROST: Fair ROundS for Threshold Signatures", PoPETs 2021 (arXiv:2020.08525); Gennaro–Goldfeder–Micali, "Threshold-optimal ECDSA", 2020; YOSO models (Blum et al., CRYPTO 2021); Groth–Ostrovsky–Sahai proactive UC (verify).
aliases: proactive threshold signatures design target; FROST with proactivity

title: Consensus with throughput-decentralization-latency all at once
open: Design a consensus protocol simultaneously achieving: >=100k TPS sustained, >=10k independent validators (no committee assumptions), <=1s finality on a WAN, and accountability (identifiable equivocation). Existing designs sit on a frontier: committees (high TPS, weak decentralization), fully-participatory DAG/BFT (decentralization, lower TPS), and no construction credibly claims all four; matching lower bounds are not known for the combined regime.
status: Hotstuff descendants + DAG-Metropolis/Narwhal-style decoupling push TPS with committees; Ethereum L1 keeps decentralization at ~10^2-10^3 TPS; Solana-style pushes latency+TPS at committee-ish hardware assumptions. Combined-envelope design open.
why: The throughput wall is the stated blocker for global-scale settlement; every major chain is a point on this frontier rather than beyond it.
key_works: Yin et al., "HotStuff", PODC 2019; Danezis et al., "Narwhal and Bullshark", SOSP 2022 (arXiv:2101.11927); Lewis-Pye et al. on DAG consensus (verify).
aliases: consensus design trilemma+; DAG BFT at global scale

title: zkVM with transparent setup, general-purpose expressiveness, and real-time proving
open: Design a zkVM (proof of correct execution of arbitrary programs) achieving simultaneously: transparent (no trusted setup — STARK-style or folding), prover overhead < 10x native execution (currently 100-10,000x), constant/small proofs, and lookup/arithmetic performance that handles both bit-twiddling and big-int workloads without circuit special-casing. No system achieves the combination; prover overhead is the binding constraint.
status: STARKs (transparent, slow provers), SNARKs with preprocessing (small proofs, trusted setup or structured), folding schemes (Nova-style — recursion amortization, still ~10^2x overhead), GPU/FPGA provers narrow but don't close the gap. 10x-overhead zkVM is a credible open design target, not a proof-fantasy.
why: Sub-10x proving would move ZK from settlement/attestation to general private/verifiable computing (databases, ML inference, games); it is the design gap between current zkVMs (Risc0, SP1, Jolt — mid-10^2 to 10^3x) and "just run it".
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al., "Scalable Zero Knowledge" (STARKs), IACR 2018; Kothapalli–Setty–Tzialla, "Nova", CRYPTO 2022 (arXiv:2111.12460); zkVM engineering lines: RISC Zero, SP1, Jolt (arXiv:2403.12987, verify); Bénabaud et al. lookup arguments (verify).

title: Complete constant-time verified Rust crypto stack
open: Build a Rust cryptography stack where every implementation is formally verified constant-time (machine-checked, not just audited): symmetric primitives, ECC/arithmetic, TLS-adjacent protocols, and the runtime beneath. Today fiat-crypto/HACL*/hacspec cover slices; no stack covers all primitives + protocol layers with verified constant-timeness end to end (secret-dependent branching/timing/cache still creeps in via build flags, generics, and allocator behavior).
status: Fiat Crypto (verified field arithmetic, no constant-time *machine code* proof in general), HACL* (verified C), hacspec2 (rustspec→F* pipeline, growing), libjade (Jasmin, verified assembly for some primitives). Coverage is partial per-primitive; a complete, maintained, fully-verified constant-time stack does not exist.
why: Timing side channels remain the #1 real-world crypto implementation vulnerability class (OpenSSL-era lessons repeating in Rust ecosystems); verification is the only durable answer.
key_works: Fiat Crypto (arXiv:1607.03887 line); Jasmin/libjade (Barthe et al.); hacspec2 (arXiv:2411.18336, verify); ct-verif/timecop/dudect tooling lines (verify).
aliases: verified constant-time library; formally timed crypto

title: Production-grade threshold cryptography library with DKG, refresh, and recovery
open: Build a maintained, production-grade Rust (or equivalent) library implementing the full threshold lifecycle — distributed key generation, proactive refresh, backup/recovery, threshold signatures (ECDSA/Schnorr/BLS) — composable across custody setups, with identifiability of aborts and adversarially-tested networking. Existing libraries implement fragments; none ships the full lifecycle as one audited, boring-to-deploy stack.
status: Fragments: tss-lib/two-party ECDSA lines, FROST implementations (frost-core and deployments), threshold BLS in ETH staking (deposit contract tooling), WebAuthn-adjacent custody systems. Full DKG+refresh+recovery+multi-scheme library with production hardening: absent.
why: Every serious custody/bridge/staking system re-implements this badly; a complete library is the difference between threshold crypto as literature and as infrastructure.
key_works: FROST (arXiv:2020.08525); Gennaro–Goldfeder DKG lines; frost-core (ZcashFrost spec, verify).

title: PIR serving at production scale
open: Build a single-server (or few-server) private information retrieval system serving production key-value stores at CDN-like latency and bandwidth overhead: billions of 32-256 byte records, p50 < 100ms query, sub-linear communication, with rate-1-approaching schemes where available. Current PIR research systems handle millions of records at best, or require heavy offline phases; no deployed general-purpose private-index service exists.
status: Research systems: OnionPIR/SealPIR (Microsoft, millions of records, ~seconds), Corpus-PIR/constant-weight PIR (faster, restricted), DPF-based distributed PIR (two non-colluding servers, closer to practical). Scale+latency+generality combination: unbuilt.
why: Privacy-preserving lookups (contact discovery, ad conversion, certificate status, password breach checks) are all currently done with leakage or trusted parties; deployed PIR changes the privacy economics of the internet.
key_works: Chor–Goldreich–Kushilevitz–Sudan 1995 (PIR); SealPIR (arXiv:1709.03552); OnionPIR; DPF two-server lines (Gilboa–Ishai, Boyle et al. function secret sharing, eprint 2015/932).
aliases: PIR at scale; private database service

title: FHE runtime for compiled workloads at interpreted-language speed
open: Build an FHE toolchain that compiles ordinary programs (Rust/C subsets, SQL, ML inference graphs) to FHE executions running within ~10-100x of plaintext interpreted speed (not today's 10^3-10^6x), with automated parameter/scheme selection (BFV/BGV/CKKS/TFHE-per-op), batching, and bootstrapping amortized by the compiler. Current compilers (Concrete, EVA, HEaaN.mlir lines) leave orders of magnitude on the table.
status: Concrete (Zama) targets ML inference with TFHE/BFV — still ~10^3x+ for general code; CKKS pipelines for inference-only niches approach 10^2x for narrow model classes. General compiled-workload FHE at 10-100x: absent.
why: Encrypted computation as a drop-in for cloud workloads (private SaaS, medical/genomic analytics, ad measurement) becomes deployable at 10-100x; below that it's demos only.
key_works: Concrete compiler (Zama, github.com/zama-ai/concrete); EVA (arXiv:1912.03174); HEaaN/CKKS (Cheon et al., arXiv:1704.03530); TFHE (arXiv:1608.06905).
aliases: practical FHE compiler; encrypted compute runtime

title: iO from one-way functions
open: Construct indistinguishability obfuscation from nothing stronger than the existence of one-way functions — the minimal plausible assumption. Current candidate iO needs bilinear maps, LWE, or CRT-style multilinear maps with strong security assumptions.
status: iO achieved from LWE-based multilinear-map-like tools (Garg–Gentry–Halevi line, 2013+), then from well-founded LWE variants (Jain–Lin–Sahai 2021+); OWF-only remains open; no impossibility known.
why: The holy grail of cryptographic obfuscation: "den Boer's dream" — obfuscation as weakly assumed as hashing; unlocks virtual black-box-ish power for all of crypto.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai, "Distinguishing-Obfuscation from LWE" (arXiv:2010.13642); Garg et al. candidate multilinear maps (eprint 2012/610); Sahai–Waters 2014 (eprint 2013/451) (verify).

title: Sound multilinear maps
open: Construct multilinear maps that resist zeroizing/averaging/nucleation attacks while supporting degree ≥ 3, with a plausible concrete-security story. All proposed maps (GGH13, CLT13, GGH15) have suffered decisive structural attacks; no current map family is considered sound.
status: GGH13 zeroizing (Cheon et al. 2015), CLT13 attacks (2020 CH ePrint line), GGH15 nucleation (Miles–Sahai–Zhandry 2016) (verify); the field awaits a surviving construction.
why: Multilinear maps were the path to general obfuscation, program obfuscation applications, and constrained PRFs; their collapse is the biggest open wound in crypto construction.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Halevi (eprint 2012/610); Coron–Lepoint–Tibouchi (2013); Cheon et al. zeroizing (Eurocrypt 2015).

title: FHE at native cost
open: FHE schemes where homomorphic operations cost (1+o(1))× plaintext operations — no bootstrapping wall, no multiplicative-depth scheduling, ciphertext expansion rate → 1. Today: 10^3-10^6x overheads with active bootstrapping management.
status: BGV/BFV/CKKS amortize well with packing but pay bootstrapping; TFHE avoids packing for fast boolean; rate-1 FHE exists for limited function classes (eprint lines, verify); general native-cost FHE: no candidate, no impossibility at the asymptotic level.
why: Encrypted computation becoming a drop-in alternative to plaintext — the difference between demos and infrastructure.
key_works: Gentry 2009 (thesis); CKKS (arXiv:1704.03530); rate-1 FHE lines (Gentry–Halevi, eprint 2019/??? verify).
aliases: bootstrapping-free FHE; rate-1 fully homomorphic encryption

title: Constant-overhead RAM MPC
open: Maliciously secure MPC for RAM programs (not circuits) with overhead independent of memory size beyond O(log n) ORAM costs, supporting dynamic data, with dishonest-majority and guaranteed output delivery or identifiable abort.
status: Circuit-model MPC is poly-overhead; RAM-MPC via ORAM adds polylog factors with big constants (Wang et al. lines, verify); constant-overhead RAM-MPC under malicious security: open.
why: Real computations are memory-bound (databases, graphs, ML); circuit-only MPC forces quadratic-ish blowups that make "MPC the database" impossible.
key_works: Gordon et al. RAM-MPC lines (CCS 2012+); ORAM (Stefanov et al., S&P 2013) (verify).

title: Transparent SNARK with constant proofs and linear-time proving
open: A zk-SNARK achieving simultaneously: transparent setup (no ceremony), O(1) proof size, prover time O(n) with small constants, and post-quantum security. STARKs give transparency+PQ but polylog proofs and quasilinear provers with heavy constants; pairing SNARKs give tiny proofs but trusted setup and non-PQ.
status: Each pair achievable; all four simultaneously: open. Folding schemes (Nova-style) move toward it via recursion but inherit hash-based prover costs.
why: The "everything SNARK": verification cheap enough for blockchains and browsers, no trust ceremony, quantum-safe.
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al. STARK (2018); Nova (arXiv:2111.12460); Bünz et al. transparent setups line (eprint 2018/646) (verify).

title: Publicly verifiable MPC
open: Design MPC where, besides privacy and robustness, ANY outsider can verify the computation was done correctly — combining MPC with ZK: parties jointly produce a succinct proof that the MPC execution on their secret shares followed the protocol, without leaking inputs. Existing verifiable-MPC lines add proofs but blow up rounds/communication.
status: Research fragments: proofs of correct shuffling/decryption (verifiable mixnets, BLS threshold proofs), zkVM-based MPC checkpoints (emerging); a general, cheap, publicly verifiable MPC framework: absent.
why: Trust-minimized multiparty services (auctions, lotteries, custody, oracles) need public auditability, not just honest-majority assurances.
key_works: verifiable mixnets (Neff 2001; Bayer–Groth 2012, arXiv:1211.3168); threshold BLS proofs; zkVM lines.
aliases: auditable MPC; MPC with public auditability

title: Verifiable computation on encrypted data (FHE × ZK)
open: Combine FHE and ZK so a cloud server proves IN ZERO KNOWLEDGE that it correctly evaluated the circuit on ciphertexts it cannot decrypt — verifiable FHE where the proof hides nothing beyond correctness. Current VC-over-FHE (PINNs, GIPs) adds significant overhead; the design target is overhead within 10x of plain FHE.
status: Gentry–Wichs impossibility separates proof-of-correctness from information-theoretic checking, but succinct ZK proofs over homomorphic ciphertexts exist at overhead; the practical combined runtime: open target.
why: The full stack of delegated encrypted compute: confidentiality (FHE) + integrity (ZK) + succinctness — "don't trust the cloud at all."
key_works: Gennaro–Gentry–Parno verifiable computation (2010); Gentry–Wichs (STOC 2011); FHE+SNARK hybrid lines (verify).

title: zkTLS / trust-minimized oracles
open: Systems proving facts about TLS-protected web sessions (account balances, API responses) to a blockchain/verifier without the website cooperating — TLS-oracle compatibility with modern handshakes (TLS 1.3, post-quantum hybrid X25519MLKEM768), replay protection, and privacy of the rest of the session. Current deployments (TLSNotary/DECO/Reclaim lines) chase a moving target as TLS evolves.
status: DECO (Zhang et al., CCS 2020), TLSNotary, Reclaim deployed on testnets/mainnets; keeping pace with PQ TLS + attested-client diversity + anti-replay: open engineering/theory frontier.
why: The bridge between web data and trustless systems — the oracle problem's most practical attack surface.
key_works: DECO (arXiv:1909.00938); TLSNotary docs; Reclaim protocol papers (verify).

title: zkVM proving LLM inference
open: Prove correct execution of a full transformer forward pass (billions of FLOPs, gigabytes of weights) inside a zkVM with total proving cost under ~$0.01 per million tokens — currently 10^4-10^6x native cost, making per-token proving economically absurd. Needs: fixed-point numerics matching GPU nondeterminism bounds, attention as lookup-friendly circuits, weight-commitment reuse across queries.
status: zkML lines (ezkl, modulus, zkLLM paper arXiv:2404.16109) prove small nets (CNNs, toy transformers); frontier LLM inference unproven at any cost; no impossibility.
why: Verifiable AI: model-card enforcement, auditable API claims ("this output came from this weights hash"), anti-fraud in AI marketplaces, scientific reproducibility of model results.
key_works: zkLLM (arXiv:2404.16109); ezkl (github.com/zkonduit/ezkl); Mystic/Morphism lines (verify).

title: Verifiable training and fine-tuning
open: Produce succinct, publicly verifiable proofs that a model was trained on a claimed dataset/compute budget (with stated hyperparameters), hiding data contents — verifiable training via proof-carrying checkpoints, SNARK-friendly training logs, or GGM-style intermediate attestations. Open at every scale above toy models.
status: Proof-carrying data lines (BTC-style inscription attestations), zkML training experiments on MNIST-scale; full pretraining verification: no approach comes within orders of magnitude; no impossibility known.
why: Regulatory and scientific claims about training data/compute (provenance, licensing, "no PII", compliance) become checkable instead of self-attested.
key_works: Abadi et al. proof-carrying data (2015, verify); zkML training demos; Jolt/SP1 zkVM benchmarks.

title: Witness encryption for all of NP from standard assumptions
open: Construct witness encryption for arbitrary NP statements from standard assumptions (LWE, or even one-way functions). Current constructions need iO (WE follows from iO) or broken multilinear maps; Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters gave the first candidate from multilinear maps (2010), and no standard-assumption construction is known for all NP.
status: WE from iO: known. From snARGs for NP in CRS form: known (Choudhuri et al., Garg–Srinivasan lines, 2017+). From LWE directly: only for specific languages (graph isomorphism, some lattice-y statements). The general standard-assumption case: open — one of the cleanest big questions in the area.
why: WE is "encryption to a condition": the public key IS a puzzle. It converts proof-of-statement into decryption capability — the primitive underneath trustless bounties, dead-man switches, and conditional coordination.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Sahai–Waters, "Candidate Indistinguishability Obfuscation and Functional Encryption for all circuits", FOCS 2013 + WE paper CRYPTO 2010; Choudhuri–Jain–Jin, "Non-Zero Sum..." (verify); Zhandry 2024 quantum WE (verify).

title: Efficient witness encryption at bounty scale
open: Witness encryption with decryption cost practical enough for bounty markets: encrypt a $1M key to "solution to problem X", thousands of parallel ciphertexts live, decryptable by anyone who finds a witness — with ciphertext size independent of statement complexity and decryption in seconds, not hours.
status: Current WE decryptors run zkSNARK-verifier-like computations; efficiency is far from bounty-market scale (each decryption = a full argument verification in the exponent). Recent SNARK-based WE (using modern provers) narrows it; sub-second decryption for large statements: open.
why: Civilizational bounty markets for theorems, vulnerabilities, algorithms, missing persons, fold-up capture-the-flag at industrial scale — WE is the load-bearing primitive.
key_works: SNARK-to-WE reductions (2017+ lines); Bhupathi et al. WE bounties (verify); Time-lock/WE hybrids.

title: Witness encryption as the universal conditional-payment substrate
open: The futures stack: WE + blockchains = conditional payments to ARBITRARY conditions (not just signature checks): pay on proof of solution, pay on future event attested by witnesses, dead-man switches, insurance payouts on verifiable conditions, prediction-market settlement to theorems, AI-agent escrow ("release funds when model M achieves benchmark B verifiably"). Design the composition standards (statement formats, witness notarization, decryption-oracle abuse prevention) that let thousands of derivative protocols build on WE.
status: Fragments exist: zkcrypt/conditional payments on chains (signature-based only), WE-based bounty demos in papers; no composability layer, no standard statement library, no decryption-abuse defenses. iO-cost WE blocks deployment today.
why: This is the 25+ derivatives platform: every escrow, bounty, bequest, insurance, milestone-payment, capture-the-flag, proof-of-reserves dispute, and AI-agent contract becomes a WE derivative once the substrate exists.
key_works: GGSW 2010; modern SNARK-based WE; Bitcoin covenants as a weaker cousin; eth auto-executing escrow discussions (verify).
